items.body: The Getaway could easily have stood on its own, but the remix sequence expands its central idea: fractured industrial sound behaving almost like an alien transmission, constantly mutating through minute edits, glitches, and rhythmic interference. Chiseled from front to back with remarkable precision The Getaway by Unterm Rad   Mike Slansky, operating as Unterm Rad, continues his run of punishing industrial IDM with The Getaway for the ever-consistent Bulgaria-based Mahorka imprint. With a background spanning audio engineering, expansive sound design, and graphic work reaching back to the Tympanik Audio era, Slansky was also a key component of the now-shuttered Point Source Electronic Arts collective. His work has long occupied darker electronic spaces, and The Getaway pushes further into that territory through an unusually constrained process: the album was composed entirely from short instrument clips and sounds supplied through Point Source’s Genome sample kits, each fragment carefully edited, processed, and sequenced until it evolved into something entirely new. No synthesizers, AI, or outside sound sources were used, adhering to the open-source spirit of the Genome project. Seven original pieces emerge as dark-grey slabs of machinery, where microscopic edits and fractured rhythms give each track a strangely extraterrestrial charge. Up front, “Hang Me Out To Dry” drives through minimal industrial fissures with a beat-heavy barrage of rugged technoid tones, metallic grit, and tightly controlled distortion. “They’re On To Us” narrows the focus further, exposing Slansky’s precision-built rhythmic glitches as tiny mechanical movements seem to twitch beneath the surface, while “Cornered” opens into broken beats and cavernous echoes, giving the record a sense of mechanical engineer​ing operating somewhere far beyond human reach. Transparent details become increasingly exposed :: The final six pieces hand Slansky’s material over to Access to Arasaka, Evaluation Copy, Vaag, Feederwire, Hexalyne, and Cole, each pulling the source tracks into a distinct interpretation. Rather than simply extending the album, these remixes reveal just how much microscopic movement exists inside Slansky’s sound structures. Access to Arasaka and Hexalyne sharpen the material into brisk, erratic sci-fi electro-nics; Evaluation Copy scorches through beats and bass; Vaag bends the rhythms into flexible broken beat contortions; and Feederwire drags everything through piercing industrial low-end vibrations. Cole’s closing interpretation is perhaps the most surreal, stripping the machinery back until its strange, transparent details become increasingly exposed. The Getaway could easily have stood on its own, but the remix sequence expands its central idea: fractured industrial sound behaving almost like an alien transmission, constantly mutating through minute edits, glitches, and rhythmic interference. Closing with “The Walls Are Closing In,” before the remixes kick in, Slansky lets pressure evaporate into sparse technoid shifts, leaving behind an album that feels both rigorously engineered and strangely alive. By opening his source material to collaborators, he turns a tightly controlled sonic experiment into a broader study of industrial texture, glitch mechanics, and extraterrestrial electronics—chiseled from front to back with remarkable precision. The Getaway is available on Mahorka. [Bandcamp] The Getaway by Unterm RadThe post Unterm Rad :: The Getaway (Mahorka) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.
items._cn_summary: 《The Getaway》由Unterm Rad（Mike Slansky）创作，完全使用Point Source Electronic Arts的Genome开源样本包中碎片化的乐器短片段，经过精细编辑、处理与序列编排而成，未使用合成器或AI。七首原始作品以工业IDM为基调，通过微观编辑与断裂节奏构建出近乎外星信号般的暗灰色机械质感，金属颗粒感与失真控制紧密咬合。专辑后半部分由Access to Arasaka、Evaluation Copy、Vaag、Feederwire、Hexalyne、Cole六位艺术家分别进行remix，各自牵引出原作内部的微观运动——从锐利科幻电子、灼热碎拍低音，到扭曲破碎节奏与超现实透明细节，多元诠释扩展了原始素材的可能性。整体呈现出受约束的工艺流程下，从有限素材中演化出的高度变异声响结构。

items.body: 33 takes the traditional age of Christ at his death as the axis of a twelve-part electroacoustic cycle concerned with creation, incarnation, suffering, death and renewal. Yara Mekawei and Amir Rezk draw on biblical passages, Coptic Orthodox liturgy and Arabic recitation, but rarely allow the texts to remain intact: voices are repeated, stretched and submerged until scripture begins to function as rhythm and texture. Dense drones, fractured percussion, recitation and sudden clearings give the record a ceremonial character without turning it into devotional music. Its structure is particularly effective. “LOGOS” begins with John’s “In the beginning was the Word”; by “New Creation,” Revelation has replaced Genesis, with the first heaven and earth passing away and death itself disappearing. Between them, “Mysterion,” “33,” “Harrowing of Hades” and “Sackcloth Love” trace a passage through Eucharist, Crucifixion, descent and mourning. Musically, 33 sits between electroacoustic composition, dark ambient, and industrial electronics with a hint of prog rock, although none of those descriptions quite accounts for its restless construction. Mekawei and Rezk work with low drones, distorted orchestral sonorities, spoken voices, granular processing and percussion that repeatedly breaks apart just as it appears to settle into a pattern. The music can be oppressively dense, then abruptly hollowed out to expose a voice or a thin electronic residue. Rather than using electronics as accompaniment to the religious texts, the pair subject voice and instrumental material to the same processes: syllables become pulses, recitation turns into noise, and acoustic sounds lose their identifiable origins. This constant movement between intelligibility and abstraction gives the album much of its tension. What begins with a private anxiety surrounding the age of 33 expands into a work about mortality and transformation, with ancient texts treated not as historical artefacts but as material that can still be sounded, fractured and inhabited. To help us further navigate the album, we reached out directly to Yara Mekawei and Amir Rezk. 33 seems to follow an unusually coherent spiritual trajectory: from the Logos and creation in “LOGOS” and “Genesis,” through embodiment, suffering and death, to resurrection and finally the New Jerusalem in “New Creation.” Yet the album never feels like a straightforward retelling of scripture; texts are fragmented, repeated, obscured and absorbed into the electronics. Did you conceive the twelve tracks as a narrative or liturgical cycle from the outset, and how important was it that this progression could be felt without necessarily being understood literally? From the very beginning, we did not set out to create a straightforward textual retelling or a literal recitation of scripture. For us, the sacred texts are not static history; they are a living, sonic score. The progression across the twelve tracks was essential because we recognized that the trajectory of Christ’s life, from incarnation and embodiment, through suffering, descent, and ultimate renewal, is not merely a historical or theological timeline. It is a universal, spiritual archetype. It is a pattern that exists in the world and plays out in our own lives, in human endurance, migration, grief, and rebirth, whether we consciously recognize it or not. By weaving Yara’s personal story, her family inheritance, her grandmother’s warning, her lived experience of displacement and transformation, into this grander framework, the album becomes a dual narrative. The fragmentation, repetition, and electronic processing of the texts reflect how personal memory and sacred history actually operate in human consciousness: rarely as a clean, linear text, but as lingering textures, echoes, and internal pictures. It was crucial that a listener could feel this emotional and spiritual weight instinctively without needing to decipher every word literally, because the underlying trajectory of endurance and transformation is something universally felt in the human spirit. The number 33 begins from something intensely personal — a maternal warning about the thirty-third year of life — but the album gradually connects that age to Christ’s suffering, death and resurrection. In the title track especially, the language of Isaiah’s suffering servant and the Crucifixion seems to make personal vulnerability and sacred history overlap. How did that private association with the age of 33 become the organising principle of the record, and did making the album change what that number meant to you? The connection became obvious the moment we realized that 33 was not just a personal chronological marker, but the darkest point in Christ’s earthly life, the threshold of Gethsemane and the Cross, where He faced an unrepeatable cup of unknown suffering and abandonment. In our own human lives, those rock-bottom moments, where we carry an unbearable personal weight or face severe displacement, often become the precise pivots for profound transformation. The warning Yara inherited about the thirty-third year was essentially pointing toward this exact kind of personal Gethsemane: a room where you are tested to your limits, forcing a parallel between our lived vulnerability and what Christ endured. Creating 33 completely changed what that number means to us. Through the process of writing and immersing ourselves in these detailed sonic patterns and raw emotions, 33 transformed from an ominous, looming warning into a symbol of profound solidarity. It fixed a truth in our minds: our suffering in this life is never meaningless, nor is it carried in isolation. The Divine chose to step into human history and share directly in our exact grief, exile, and pain. Through making this record, the thirty-third year ceased to be a room of fear, becoming instead a reminder that we are never truly alone in the dark. Sacred language in 33 occupies a strange position between meaning and sound. Biblical passages, Coptic Orthodox material, Arabic and other vocal fragments can initially be intelligible, but repetition and electronic processing often push them toward rhythm, texture or something resembling incantation. Yara, your previous work has already explored ways of translating sacred texts into sonic structures; how did the two of you approach the voice here? Were you interested in preserving the theological meaning of these texts, or in reaching a point where the sound of devotion itself becomes the compositional material? For us, it was never a choice between preserving theological meaning or turning the text into pure abstraction, we wanted both. We approached the sacred texts as both a coherent narrative framework and a stream of subconscious thought, treating the voice as a primary musical texture. We deeply respect the inherent power of music to imprint a specific fingerprint upon the mind and the soul. However, we wouldn’t use the word “incantation” to describe this process. Instead, we see the voice and its electronic transformations as a sonic blessing carried through the physical sound waves themselves. We knew that many people listening across the world wouldn’t understand Arabic or Coptic, but we believed that sound itself can transcend language barriers. By layering, repeating, and processing these sacred fragments, we wanted to carry the spiritual energy and raw devotion directly to the listener’s intuition. The theological meaning grounds the structure, while the sonic vibration allows the blessing to reach anyone who listens, regardless of whether they can translate the words. There is a striking circularity between the beginning and end of the album. “LOGOS” opens with John’s “In the beginning was the Word,” while “New Creation” ultimately arrives at Revelation’s vision of the first heaven and earth passing away, God wiping away every tear, and death ceasing to exist. Between those points, the music moves through creation, the body, Eucharist, suffering, mourning and resurrection. Do you think of 33 as moving from one creation to another — and, if so, is “new creation” primarily a Christian theological idea for you, or does it also describe a personal process of destruction and transformation that took place while making the record? It is deeply both: a personal process of transformation and a theological truth made manifest. On a personal and artistic level, 33 is our very first collaboration together, so the album itself is literally a “new creation” born from our two individual musical worlds. We share the belief that marrying the arts with the sacred is like bringing heaven and earth together, much like the Incarnation of the Divine Logos coming down to breathe new life into His creation and bloom into a new Tree of Life. J.R.R. Tolkien spoke of artists as “sub-creators” or co-creators alongside the Great Creator. By deliberately inviting the Divine into our sound, making a “new creation” was never about trying to invent a new genre of music; it was about marrying the eternal with the earthly, which makes the work spiritual and new at its core. Making this album was an essential process of bringing light directly into the desolation of our own personal suffering and “stations” of life. It was a way to ground those difficult experiences in hope and meaning, not just for ourselves, but hopefully for anyone who listens to the record. (Gianmarco Del Re)
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以基督受难年龄三十三岁为轴心，构建十二部分的电声循环，从逻各斯与创世出发，经由道成肉身、圣餐、受难、死亡与哀悼，最终抵达新天新地。阿拉伯艺术家Mekawei与Rezk将科普特正教礼仪、阿拉伯诵读与圣经经文作为声音素材，通过重复、拉伸、颗粒化处理，使语言消解为节奏与质感。专辑横跨电声作曲、暗氛围与工业电子，低频嗡鸣、失真管弦音色、破碎打击乐与突然的留白交替出现，电子处理平等对待人声与乐器材料。专辑呈现私人焦虑如何扩展为对死亡与转化的冥想，古代文本在此被重新激活、碎片化并被当代声音所栖居。

items.body: Arshan Najafi‘s Zenosyne takes its title from John Koenig’s neologism describing the unsettling sensation that time seems to accelerate as we grow older. The album focuses on the paradox behind that sensation. As Najafi explains in the accompanying interview, the music emerged from a period in which he felt psychologically frozen while time rushed relentlessly onwards. This tension between stillness and acceleration defines the album’s two long-form electroacoustic compositions. Built from live improvisations using a piezo microphone attached to an external hard drive alongside the sonification of raw digital data, Zenosyne makes surprisingly little ceremony of its unusual sound sources. The hard drive becomes another resonant object, its vibrations feeding a semi-generative system that Najafi actively steers. Algorithmic processes introduce an element of instability, but his intervention remains central to the shape of the music. The opening “Binary Bloom” begins with almost imperceptible movement. Sustained electronic tones slowly develop interference patterns and harmonic beating, gathering momentum from within. Energy and apparent speed continue to increase without reaching a conventional climax, and the accumulated tension eventually dissipates. “Static Rotation” expands this language through a more active dialogue between pure tone and electronic noise. Its materials circulate around an unstable centre, creating perpetual motion with little sense of arrival. Najafi places considerable trust in microscopic change. Much of the musical activity remains concentrated in the lower and middle registers. Rhythm and dramatic contrast play relatively small roles, while subtle redistributions of spectral energy, minute shifts in timbre and constantly evolving resonances determine the form. Musical time is stretched sufficiently for these small changes to acquire unusual weight, sharpening our awareness of its passing. To get an idea of Arshan Najafi’s live process, here is a recording of one of his no-input mixer and computer sets, followed by an interview about the making of Zenosyne. Zenosyne takes its title from John Koenig’s neologism and yet the album doesn’t seem to represent memory nostalgically. Instead, both “Binary Bloom” and “Static Rotation” seem to suspend chronological time altogether, creating spaces in which microscopic changes become more significant than linear progression. How did the idea of Zenosyne shape your compositional thinking? Were you interested in evoking the psychological sensation of accelerated time, or in constructing an alternative temporal experience in which conventional notions of duration begin to dissolve? I chose the title Zenosyne because it perfectly captured my state of mind during the composition process and still does. I was experiencing this overwhelming feeling of staying completely still – almost a sense of uselessness or incapability – while watching every day pass by in a flash of light. The music reflects that paradox. The suspension of linear time you noticed in these pieces wasn’t necessarily a conceptual design to challenge musical duration, but rather a direct mirror of that personal, psychological standstill. It is the feeling of being frozen in place while time accelerates around you. Your previous releases, from Imaginary Crisis to Live at Daa Theater House, have consistently explored live electronics, improvisation and the instability of sound in performance. Zenosyne continues that trajectory, drawing on live recordings made with a piezo microphone placed on an external hard drive alongside the sonification of raw digital data. What attracted you to treating a storage device not simply as a technological object but as a resonant instrument? Did working with the physical vibrations of digital memory alter the way you think about the relationship between information, sound and materiality? I have to admit, the reason is a bit less poetic than treating the drive as a metaphor for digital memory! I have a habit of attaching piezo mics to anything that I basically can. Frankly, I don’t see much point in recording traditional acoustic instruments anymore. That’s one of the main points of electronic music for me: it obliterates the need for conventional instruments. It gives us the freedom to choose the most mundane surface or object as a sound source and manipulate it into an entirely new form. The hard drive was just a fascinating object to harvest raw frequencies from, which the computer then allows me to further process. Both pieces were improvised live in Max/MSP before being shaped during the mixing process in Ableton Live. Listening to the album, there is a constant negotiation between systems that appear algorithmic and gestures that feel spontaneous or instinctive. How do you understand improvisation when working with generative processes? Do you see yourself directing the system, collaborating with it, or responding to behaviours that emerge unexpectedly during performance? I definitely see myself as the director of the system. I design a semi-generative algorithmic environment that responds to incoming signals based on parameters I’ve dictated beforehand. I call it “semi-generative” because I intentionally build it to a point where it still requires my interaction to continue its work; it cannot sustain itself without being steered and not sound boring to me. I view live improvisation fundamentally as a technique of composing on the fly. Because there are physical, unpredictable elements – like the random fluctuations of the hard disk spinning in “Static Rotation” – I have to remain hyper-aware and react to sudden gestures, not to mention I often cause those sudden gestures myself because I feel it’s needed at that particular moment. It’s a constant dialogue between the rules I set and the behavior the system throws back at me. Your work moves fluidly between sound, image and text—you are not only a composer but also the author of Twenty Wrong Turns. Across these different media there seems to be a recurring interest in fragmentation, ambiguity and the ways meaning emerges from incomplete information. Does Zenosyne belong to that same broader artistic inquiry? More generally, how do writing and sound composition inform one another in your practice, and are there ideas that can only be explored through one medium rather than the other? To be completely honest, I haven’t consciously intertwined my music and my writing so far. I tend to treat them as separate practices that serve different purposes. However, the connection that I do see between these mediums is the word “composition” itself, as I fundamentally treat them the same way. That’s the whole point for me. While they usually exist on their own, I might occasionally bring them together – it really just depends on how I feel about a certain project. (Gianmarco Del Re)
items._cn_summary: 专辑以"Zenosyne"（时间随年龄加速流逝之感）为概念，由两首长篇电声作品构成。声音素材来自压电麦克风拾取外置硬盘的物理振动以及原始数字数据的声化处理，硬件本身被当作共鸣体纳入半生成系统。作者在算法过程与主动操控之间保持平衡，使听感在静态与加速之间持续张力。"Binary Bloom"从几乎不可感知的电子长音起始，干扰模式与谐波拍频缓慢堆积，能量不断上升却回避传统高潮；"Static Rotation"则在纯音与电子噪声之间展开更活跃的对话，材料围绕不稳定核心循环往复。作品聚焦低频与中频区段，节奏与戏剧性对比被刻意压缩，取而代之的是频谱能量的微观再分配、音色的细微偏移与持续演化的共鸣。时间被充分拉伸，微小变化获得异常分量，促使听众重新感知时间流逝本身。

items.excerpt: The Bug’s Ladybug 2 pairs his heavy, hypnotic bass pressure with Friday Night Plans’ hushed vocals, turning six versions of “Miss U” into a dark, immersive journey where dub, shoegaze, and electronic melancholy slowly dissolve into one hypnotic flow. items.body: The Bug’s Ladybug 2 pairs his heavy, hypnotic bass pressure with Friday Night Plans’ hushed vocals, turning six versions of “Miss U” into a dark, immersive journey where dub, shoegaze, and electronic melancholy slowly dissolve into one hypnotic flow. Bass pressure meets quiet melancholy Ladybug 2 by The Bug / Friday Night Plans   The second chapter in the Ladybug series arrives just over a month after The Bug’s encounter with Dis Fig. The premise remains intact: Kevin Richard Martin entrusts his universe of bass pressure and deceleration to a different female voice, allowing each contact to alter its direction. This time the chosen presence is Friday Night Plans, the project led by Japanese vocalist Masumi. In 2023, Martin named Visitors his album of the year; three years later, that act of listening becomes a collaboration, taking shape in the six variations of Miss U released by Pressure. The artwork anticipates the character of the record. Masumi’s face, hidden behind dark glasses, emerges from a field of weathered white, almost erased by a layer of photographic dust. The music also withholds any sharp definition. Her voice feels close and already remote, the rhythm distorts the perception of time, while the bass presses forward relentlessly and casts a dim light around itself. This is sound that narcotizes, shifts the center of listening and carries the listener elsewhere through a calm troubled by unease. Miss U is approached six times, through reductions and deformations that alter the weight of its individual elements. Martin works with recurrence, with the memory of what has just been heard, with the expectation of an impact that may arrive late or dissolve entirely. The Broken versions sharpen this logic: the song loses its outline and enters a haze where dub meets the languor of shoegaze and certain strains of electronic mel​ancholy from the nineties. Keyboards float, the central matter grows rough, the foundation preserves an enormous power. Everything moves slowly and with absolute discipline, even when it seems close to collapse. Masumi avoids any display of force. Her singing is hushed, melancholy, almost oblique; it brings a controlled fragility into a sound system capable of swallowing her whole. That disparity feeds the attraction of Ladybug 2. Her voice skims the surfaces, disappears for long stretches, then returns like a thought that sleep had only hidden. Martin gives her a simple and memorable melodic line, surrounding it with echoes and deep expanses of absence. The result retains a secret pop element, perceptible even in its most disintegrated forms. “Masumi allows herself to be absorbed, becoming color and breath, encouraging an unbroken hypnotic continuity. The first volume moved through successive intensifications; this one favours dissolution.” ~Mirco Salvadori The comparison with Ladybug 1 is unavoidable and clarifies the distinct character of these two episodes. With Dis Fig, the voice seemed to act from inside the music, pushing each version towards a further degree of emotional exposure. Vanishing carried the weight of a wound spoken aloud; its subsequent mutations extended the narrative and allowed new tensions to emerge. Friday Night Plans adopts a more elusive presence. Masumi allows herself to be absorbed, becoming color and breath, encouraging an unbroken hypnotic continuity. The first volume moved through successive intensifications; this one favors dissolution. From that choice arise both the record’s particular allure and its mildest limitation. Ladybug 2 possesses an extraordinary sensory pull, wrapping itself around the body and suspending thought; across the sequence, its emotional transformations feel less profound than those heard in the previous chapter. Some versions extend a state that has already been achieved, refining the same vertigo and adjusting its density. The experience continues to seduce as the journey assumes a more circular form. There is less risk, less drama, and a reduced ability to change meaning with each passage. It would be unfair to read this restraint as fatigue. Martin is defining a series built upon the responses of different voices to his musical grammar, and Ladybug 2 demonstrates how readily that language can welcome distant sensibilities. The production has an almost tactile precision. The bass takes on physical dimensions, pauses open sudden drops, vocal fragments cross the mass with exhausted grace. Even the most rarefied moments maintain their pressure. The music seduces through a stubborn slowness and transforms repetition into an act of conscious surrender. “Its six forms construct a single dark, sensual and estranging flow, from which the listener emerges with the sense of having lost contact with the outside world for a while” ~Mirco Salvadori Ladybug 1 therefore retains a slight advantage. It possessed a clearer emotional center and a dialogue between voice and sound capable of producing new consequences. Ladybug 2 chooses a more uniform beauty, less lacerating and entrusted to immersion. Its six forms construct a single dark, sensual and estranging flow, from which the listener emerges with the sense of having lost contact with the outside world for a while. It is an intensely realized work, meticulous throughout, endowed with a force that grows with the volume and with the willingness to surrender to its pace. The highest point in the series still belongs to the first encounter. This second episode broadens the design and changes the path taken by the voice. The Bug and Friday Night Plans deliver a record capable of numbing and transporting, less devastating than its predecessor and equally serious in the pursuit of its own spell. Ladybug 2 prolongs the moment following the impact, when the senses slow down and reality loses its clarity. It finds its truth there, within a submerged melancholy that keeps pulsing in silence. Ladybug 2 is available on Pressure. [Bandcamp] Ladybug 2 by The Bug / Friday Night PlansThe post The Bug / Friday Night Plans :: Ladybug 2 (Pressure) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.
items._cn_summary: The Bug的Ladybug 2是其低音压力系列第二章，与日本音乐人Friday Night Plans（Masumi）合作，以六种变体反复解构歌曲《Miss U》。专辑延续Kevin Richard Martin标志性的低频压迫感与减速美学，但策略从第一辑的逐步强化转为缓慢消解。Masumi的人声低沉克制、近乎呢喃，在厚重音场中似隐似现，与Dub的深邃空间感、九十年代电子忧郁气质及Shoegaze的朦胧质感相互渗透。编曲上通过元素的反复削减与变形，制造出一种麻醉式的聆听体验：节奏扭曲时间感知，贝斯持续推进却包裹在微弱光晕中，键盘漂浮其上，整体维持着高度自律的缓慢流动。作品在解构最深处仍保留隐秘的流行旋律线条，使瓦解与凝聚力达成微妙平衡。这是一张关于记忆、回响与缺席的专辑，声音如沉睡中隐匿又浮现的思绪。

items.body: When the final sound fades, the small white emblem at the bottom of the cover comes to mind. A wave reduced to calligraphy, discreet while the blue occupies everything. Wind Paths works in much the same way: it passes through the listener, leaves behind a faint vibration and entrusts the air with carrying it away. A form capable of appearing and dissolving within a few minutes Wind Paths by Philippe Deschamps   The cover already offers a statement of intent. A shifting blue, crossed by pale brushstrokes, occupies the entire field, leaving a small white mark near the lower edge. It could be water observed at close range, air made visible, a photograph taken in motion during a crossing. The image refuses to settle. Wind Paths follows the same impulse, entrusting its identity to whatever passes, bends and changes density. Philippe Deschamps gathers wind, waves and rain into music that is brief and lucid, animated by a calm that retains its sense of movement. Four pieces and just over ten minutes form a single current. The compact running time keeps every element clear of decorative contemplation. The chords move slowly, changing color by small degrees; the guitar disperses its outlines; the synthesizers hold open an even light, gently varied from within. The field recordings enter the wider fabric discreetly. Sea and rain shed their role as illustrative background and become pressure, an irregular pulse, a measure beyond human intention. The record listens to the landscape as it transforms it. The new gesture lies in the voice. Deschamps trained as a Baroque countertenor and draws on that experience here, freeing it from text. The vocal tones stretch, overlap and take on the quality of warm currents. No phrase reaches for​ meaning. The body emerges through breath, then merges with guitar and recorded air. This fusion forms the emotional centre of the EP. It offers a fragile presence. The listener recognises a human figure and immediately watches it dissolve into the broader movement. It is a simple decision on paper, decisive in its effect. Deschamps’ path has been leading towards this synthesis for some time. Introduced to the piano as a child, later a singer, bassist and guitarist in rock and post rock groups, then trained in film sound at La Fémis, the French composer has developed an ambient body of work since 2022, nourished by natural phenomena and mental images. “Blue Baths,” “Forest of my Nights,” “The Silence of Pallas,” “Remember the Clouds,” “Endless Vanishing Lines,” and “Entering the Ocean” mark the stages of a coherent inquiry. Ocean, sky, darkness and distance provide a different organizing principle each time. Wind Paths distils that inquiry even further. The voice enters the frame and alters the relationship between landscape and memory. Intensity develops through accumulation and minute alteration :: His experience in cinema emerges through the precision of each entrance and fade. Deschamps understands the weight of a sound placed an instant earlier or later, and knows how to let a detail acquire prominence without demanding it. Here, that sensitivity produces a fluid montage. Forms follow one another through affinity, carried by a slow pulse that resembles breathing and, at times, the movement of the tide. There are no spectacular peaks, refrains or turns designed to reclaim the listener’s attention. Intensity develops through accumulation and minute alteration. At certain points, a low line supports the entire field; elsewhere, the texture grows lighter and the voice seems to arrive from an immeasurable distance. Few materials, carefully chosen. The record’s ambient purity grows from this economy. Its sound world possesses body and depth, and maintains an almost tactile transparency. Silence appears within the gaps and along the fading edges of notes. Even the fuller passages leave an open area where the wind around the listener, distant traffic or movement elsewhere in the house can still be heard. The music welcomes such intrusions. Its open character encourages a porous relationship with the present. Wind Paths can drift at low volume and preserve its identity; under closer listening, it reveals subtle changes, harmonies slipping sideways and voices layered with restraint. Such control brings its own risk. At times, the music’s gentleness brushes against a beauty held too safely, polished until friction and surprise have almost disappeared. Its brevity sharpens the issue: certain openings withdraw just as they acquire an unexpected inflection. The ending arrives early and leaves a desire for one further stretch, perhaps a little less serene. This limitation also clarifies the nature of the project. Wind Paths chooses a form capable of appearing and dissolving within a few minutes. It asks for attention without insisting upon it. The title speaks of invisible paths, and the music realizes that idea with remarkable coherence. Each element follows its own direction, guided by shared currents. The voice rises, the guitar fades, the harmonies change their angle. Deschamps has created one of his most lucid works, bringing together his vocal training, cinematic sensibility and ambient practice within a form that feels accessible, intimate and precise. When the final sound fades, the small white emblem at the bottom of the cover comes to mind. A wave reduced to calligraphy, discreet while the blue occupies everything. Wind Paths works in much the same way: it passes through the listener, leaves behind a faint vibration and entrusts the air with carrying it away. Wind Paths is available on Silent Sonic. items._cn_summary: Philippe Deschamps 的《Wind Paths》是一部仅四曲、十分钟出头的短篇氛围作品，以风声、海浪、雨声等田野录音为底色，将巴洛克假声男高音训练中习得的人声从文本中解放，转化为与合成器、吉他、空气声交织的呼吸质感。评论指出，唱片的核心手法在于克制：和弦缓慢移位、吉他轮廓弥散、合成器维持均匀光源般的低饱和底色，田野录音则从装饰性的背景升格为不可预测的压力与脉搏。视觉设计与声音策略形成同构——封面上大片蓝色被一道接近书法的白色痕迹打破，作品本身也以人类气质的短暂显形随即被更广阔的运动吞噬作为情感中心。评论追溯了作者从钢琴、摇滚与后摇滚贝斯手、电影声音设计训练到 2022 年以来的环境音乐脉络，将其视为长期对自然现象与心理意象探索的进一步蒸馏，声音与记忆的关系因人声的介入而发生改变。

items.body: Giulio Aldinucci has made an album that seems acquainted with the unnamed part of human nature, the part that surfaces in sleep or in the few seconds before news capable of changing the course of a day. Rhythm is felt through changes in pressure Materia by GIULIO ALDINUCCI   At first there is weight. A quiet, almost geological pressure that arrives before recognition, touching the body before it reaches the mind. Materia begins in that dark place. Sound has volume, temperature, even something resembling a will of its own. It advances slowly and alters the scale of things, like a sudden bank of fog moving in. Sight loses its authority and the ear becomes a larger organ. Giulio Aldinucci has made an album that seems acquainted with the unnamed part of human nature, the part that surfaces in sleep or in the few seconds before news capable of changing the course of a day. The composer, born in Siena, Tuscany, reaches this point after years devoted to landscape, memory and the voice stripped of semantic meaning. The experience developed under the name Obsil and the chapter that began with Tarsia have shaped a coherent body of work, nourished by field recordings, choral presences and electronic transformations. Borders And Ruins examined the nature of territory; Disappearing In A Mirror and Shards Of Distant Times shifted the tension towards identity and memory; Real sought a personal reality within the excess of digital mediation. Materia, Aldinucci’s fifth album for Karlrecords, condenses that history into an essential gesture: taking a tightly packed mass of sound, carving into it, paring it back and searching for what is already alive​ inside. The album was released on September 18, 2026. Here accumulation and subtraction become emotional acts. Aldinucci gathers frequencies as scattered memories might be gathered after years apart, then removes the excess and listens into the space left behind by what has disappeared. Time, too, acquires substance. It is broken into minute units and reassembled according to an order that escapes the familiar pulse. Rhythm is felt through changes in pressure, through inner tides, through the way a distant voice rises from the haze and immediately loses its face. These are slow movements filled with secret life. Their apparent stillness is alive with motion. The six pieces form a single body lasting just under 43 minutes. Density remains the active principle, capable of changing state while retaining its gravity. The depths below sustain the journey with a telluric continuity. Above them appear distorted choirs, echoes, drifting particles and sounds that preserve a human trace after language and origin have fallen away. The titles sketch a constellation of absence: “Not Here,” the shadow cast by noise, ash and distant waves, the absolute finality of “Never,” evening, then light caught in a dream. The music receives these images and preserves their indeterminacy. Each one works within the act of listening, removed from plot and close to the freedom of involuntary association. “Materia finds its human center here. The album’s grandeur springs from this dizzying proportion: an immense sound holds a tiny gesture, perhaps a mouth drawing breath, perhaps a syllable worn away by time.” ~Mirco Salvadori The voice is central. It rises like a collective memory without face or biography, suspended between comfort and alarm. At times it resembles someone calling across an immense distance; elsewhere it takes on the substance of a thought formed in the body before words. Aldinucci understands the power of vocal fragments and frees them from any narrative duty. What remains is breath, impulse, a tremor that reminds the listener of human fragility. Materia finds its human center here. The album’s grandeur springs from this dizzying proportion: an immense sound holds a tiny gesture, perhaps a mouth drawing breath, perhaps a syllable worn away by time. “Come Luce, In Sogno,” chosen as the advance single, offers a discreet way into the album. The light invoked by its title contains dust and density. It filters through opaque layers and produces figures already moving towards dissolution. Dreaming becomes a mode of knowledge. A detail can expand until it fills the entire field of perception, while an enormous event contracts into a brief vibration. This instability runs through the whole work. Time seems to lengthen; then an almost imperceptible shift alters the landscape. Sound retains warmth and a question that has yet to find words. The cover helps reveal the character of the work. A white façade multiplies concave modules, dark openings and curves that look identical only at a glance. The eye finds order, then differences, shadows, stains and minor signs of wear. It is a serial form made vulnerable by time and by the material from which it is built. Aldinucci’s music behaves in much the same way. It turns repetition into change, raises immense structures and allows irregularity to bring them alive. Each surface hints at another depth. No answer comes. The desire to look again grows stronger. The concentration of the sound demands complete attention. A moment’s distraction can break the spell, and some passages deliberately court saturation. This is an exacting choice. Materia requires time, an appropriate volume and a measure of solitude. In return it offers a rare experience, moving listening beyond taste and into consciousness. Its forms entrust their appeal to a slower force, like the memory of a place never visited. There is familiarity and a faint fear. The unknown takes on an intimate temperature. “Sound appears as something that precedes its maker and continues beyond its listener, bound to the same matter as bodies, air and thought.” ~Mirco Salvadori Throughout Aldinucci’s career, recording the world has carried the value of a living archive. A landscape could hold a story; a procession could deliver into the present voices already receding into the distance; an ordinary noise could open a passage through perception. Materia brings this practice close to an elemental dimension. Here substance comes before place and contact before narrative. Sound appears as something that precedes its maker and continues beyond its listener, bound to the same matter as bodies, air and thought. This is where its power lies. The album speaks of the human condition through feeling. The need to give chaos a shape meets the fascination of whatever resists a final form. Every cut removes part of the original mass; subtraction reveals an unforeseen outline. The music breathes between these impulses, tightens, withdraws and fills out again. At times it seems about to disclose something. Then that something changes substance and becomes pure listening. Materia is expansive, gathered into a fierce intensity and charged with physical mystery. Giulio Aldinucci reaches one of the most mature expressions of his artistic language and gives contemporary ambient music an album with moral as well as sonic weight. When the final vibration ends, silence feels altered, thicker, almost conscious. Within that silence passes an intuition that cannot quite be held: perhaps the human spirit is precisely this restless substance, seeking form while knowing that every form is temporary. For just under 43 minutes, Materia gives it a body and lets it sing. Materia is available on Karlrecords. [Bandcamp] Materia by GIULIO ALDINUCCIThe post Giulio Aldinucci :: Materia (Karlrecords) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.
items._genre: ambient / experimental electronic / drone / field recording / contemporary classical
items._cn_summary: Giulio Aldinucci 的第五张专辑《Materia》凝聚了他多年来对景观、记忆与人声的探索。整张专辑围绕「密度」这一核心原则展开：声音被压缩成紧密的质量，再经雕琢与削减，揭示内部已有的生命。节奏通过压力的变化与内在的潮汐来感知，而非传统脉冲。作品中混杂着扭曲的合唱、回声、漂浮的粒子，以及语言与源头消散后仍保留人类痕迹的声响。专辑以缓慢的动作为主，在地质般的连续性中推进，六首曲目构成一个持续约四十三分钟的整体。标题勾勒出一组关于缺席的星座：噪音、灰烬、远浪投下的阴影，以及「永不」的绝对终结。声音在减法与积累之间运作，将模糊性保留为情感的容器。

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — An unusual yet fully-progressive undertaking of setting literary stories to music using jazz-fusion artists.1. "The Sinking Spell" (4:40) Robert Wyatt's distinctive voice enters with some effect applied while the four musicians, Steve Swallow, Jack DeJohnette, Carla Bley, and Terje Rypdal apply their talents to constructing a loose and reactive soundtrack to Robert's rendering of this Edward Gorey story. Terje is particularly flamboyant (almost in a Steve Hackett way!) while Carla, Steve, and Jack are pretty dynamic in their own right. Perhaps Robert's best, most unique performance on the album and maybe the best collective Jazz-Rock Fusionary exposition as well. (9.125/10) 2. "The Object Lesson" (5:00) piano, bass and swelling cymbal crashes back Robert's rather flat/monotone delivery of this story. Eventually the musicians fall into a kind of groove with Jack DeJohnette's rock drumming and Terje Rypdal and Carla Bley's Canterbury organ saw-like expressions. The music is not great, not fully-formed or composed for much other than dramatic support, but it works (it's better than the story being told). (8.75/10)3 "The Insect God" (5:00) some truly top-notch Jazz-Rock Fusion is used to present another sobering and not-for-children's-ears story. The music quartet of Bley, Rypdal, Swallow, and drummer Jack DeJohnette are all on the same page of aggressive and insistent delivery while Robert and spoken-word "backing vocalists" render their fast-talking approach to dramatic story-telling. (8.75/10)4 "The Doubful Guest" (4:45) finally! some thoroughly-composed music! It's a challenging weave of off-timed hi-speed drum and keyboard music in which Steve and Terje contribute long-held, pensive notes on their respective instruments. All the while Robert delivers a near-spoken word story with a little more flair and enthusiasm than the past two. The overall weave really works--has no glaring flaws or inconsistencies. I like the way the musical performances ramp up toward the end: especially Terje's guitar shredding and Carla's breadth of synth strings chords. (9.125/10)5 "The Remembered Visit" (6:25) voice with syncopated bass and synth-strings pulses, adding piano and Mellotron "ooo"s and "aaah"s, then treated electric guitar notes and some background drumming. In the third minute the drums and bass play get more animated--still orchestral and reactive, though, more than "song" oriented. Where Robert's delivery starts out dramatic and engaged, it begins to sound a bit like rote reading in places. But then things slow down for the background vocal-supported passage in the fifth minute--which has the effect of seeming to bring Robert back into the spirit of the story. From there out he feels fully-present in his story-telling. Effective. (8.875/10)6 "The Hapless Child" (7:00) Robert Wyatt's distinctive voice and vocal/story-telling stylings are here backed by music that feels more like theater music: it's incidental and yet has a personality all its own--as if taking on the characteristics of Robert's story's characters. Nothing is flowing or timed, almost all of it feels impressionistic and reactive more than composed and prescribed. There is one theme that feels prepared: the whole-band motif that starts at 2:58 when Robert starts singing about the start of Charlotte Sophia's boarding school experience, but at 4:20 everything devolves to simple piano--just before launching into a more dynamic and drum-and-guitar-driven theme. What a horrifying Dickensian tale! Carla Bley's odd chord choices hold the whole thing down but it's Steve Swallow's obtuse bass notes and Terje Rypdal's sharp, stinging guitar notes that bring forth and amplify the Poe-like atmosphere of the story. Wow! What an experience! Definitely not your typical bed-time story! Even children's theatre would be scarred and marred for decades if they brought children in to hear this one! Still, it is a rather powerful and effective delivery mechanism. (13.25/15)Total Time:I have to admit that I was not prepared for either the album's total dedication to story telling nor it's dark and rather dismal, even desolate, Dickensian/Brothers Grimm/Edgar Allen Poe story lines. While I love the literate nature of the stories, I'm a bit disturbed by their unsettling subject matters. At the same time, I appreciate these adventurous musicians for their commitment to the expansion of that which music and Jazz-Rock Fusion can do. B/four stars; though admirable to take on such an odd and ambitious undertaking, I feel that the stories and music do not always match as well as the artists/producers may have wanted. Nor are the instrumental performances and song/soundtrack compositions as polished and coordinated as well as one might expect or desire from this stellar line-up.

items._cn_summary: 迈克尔·曼特勒1976年专辑《The Hapless Child and Other Inscrutable Stories》将爱德华·戈瑞的怪诞文学作品与爵士融合音乐并置，邀请罗伯特·怀亚特、卡洛·布莱、特里耶·吕普达尔、史蒂夫·斯沃洛和杰克·德约翰内特等跨领域音乐人参与演绎。作品以人声叙事为骨架，四重奏以反应式、即兴化的方式构建配乐，钢琴、低音提琴、鼓组与吉他交织出不规则节拍与音色层次。专辑在叙事节奏与器乐推进之间寻找平衡，既有松散的自由即兴段落，也有结构更趋完整的器乐织体。整张专辑呈现出戏剧配乐式的剧场感，音乐服务于文学叙事而非作为独立作品存在，同时融入了坎特伯雷派键盘音色与早期合成器弦乐铺陈，是一次文学与爵士融合的大胆跨界实验。

items.body: With Hor-Cheret, we welcome a new project presented as a collaboration between members of Vortex, Nam-Khar, and Delta Komplex, complemented by a few more artists. The project’s name alludes to Horus, the child of Isis and Osiris in Egyptian mythology. With an album title referring to an ancient nomadic law of hospitality, Hor-Cheret offers an intriguing metaphor and, in my view, a critical perspective on today’s world. It certainly offers food for thought, but above all, this is music to be discovered. From the very first notes, a distinct Ritual influence emerges through the percussion and the use of traditional acoustic instruments. While the percussion reinforces the album’s ritualistic character, the listener gradually discovers a dark atmosphere shaped by deep sound waves. Elements of Dark-Ambient and Industrial music are clearly present. An Ethereal female voice occasionally takes on a narrative role while simultaneously enhancing the sense of mysticism. The male voice also serves a narrative function, while some of the lyrics possess a distinctly poetic quality. This is a superbly crafted album in a genre that suffers from a lack of quality projects and inconsistent production standards. Hor-Cheret’s debut is a release to be savored and cherished. (Rating:8½). Listen to “In The Shadow Ov Power”: In The Shadow Ov Power by HOR-CHERET About Hor-Cheret Hor-Cheret is a new collaborative project pairing members of Vortex, Nam-Khar and Delta Komplex with additional contributors, presented on Dunkelheit Produktionen. Its name references Horus, the child of Isis and Osiris in Egyptian mythology. Nam-Khar is the ritual ambient project of Romanian musician Konchog Gyaltsen, active since 2009, previously paired with Vortex on “Nag-Hammadi” in 2022 and “The Sarajevo Spiral” in 2024. Delta Komplex is a German electronic band founded in 2019 around Minu-Schirin Samimi and Tufana, known for the 2022 album “Veils”. “Nanawatai”, Hor-Cheret’s debut album, was released on 7 November 2025 in a limited handnumbered digipak edition.

items._cn_summary: Hor-Cheret是Vortex、Nam-Khar与Delta Komplex成员的合作项目，专辑名取自古游牧民族待客之道，以隐喻方式对当代世界提出批判。从开篇起，传统打击乐与原声乐器即确立仪式基调，深层声波逐渐铺陈出黑暗氛围，融合暗潮、工业与黑暗环境声响元素。女声偶尔承担叙事功能并强化神秘感，男声同样具有叙述性质，部分歌词展现出明显的诗歌特质。这是一张在品质参差、佳作稀缺的仪式暗潮领域中精心打磨的作品，融合多国音乐人协作视角与埃及神话意象，为听众提供可反复品味的听觉体验。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.
items.label: Cool Waters
items._genre: folktronica / world fusion / experimental electronic / afro-futurism
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由德国出生、肯尼亚驻地的打击乐手Sven Kacirek与年轻搭档Olith Ratengo，以及83岁的传统肯尼亚dodo歌唱家Ogoya Nengo共同完成。Kacirek的Buchla合成器、手打打击乐与套鼓构成器乐底色，人声在其上自由交织而不被淹没。乐评特别分析了'Bara'一曲的层次建构方式：从廉价的重复节拍起始，逐步加入4/4敲击声、气泡般低频与木琴质感，合成复节奏以几乎不可察觉的方式层层堆叠，至曲末浑然一体，仿佛一直藏于人声之下。'Sarah'一曲则以Ratengo主唱，Kacirek试探性的碎拍打击与不时渗入的锐利失真回应声线的紧迫感。文章将此音乐置于'folktronica'脉络中，与Chouk Bwa及Nyege Nyege厂牌作品并置，强调其全球性与非洲根基的并存：传统成为前卫，前卫看似古老千年。Nengo以八十三岁高龄随这支以电子节奏为核心的二人组巡演并完成全球首秀，本身即为文化交融的注脚。

items.album: Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari
items.artist: Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy
items.excerpt:
Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release,
Under an Endless Sky
.
In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari,
Songs of Compassion
is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics.
Francesco Paolo Paladi
items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items._cn_summary: Tako Toki 乐队以手工自制乐器为核心特色，所有演奏乐器均由废旧物品改造而成，包括 tassofons、kitchenofon、didjerimou 等自创名称的装置。乐评重点强调这些非常规乐器在现代录音技术下仍能保持精准音高与丰富音质。在音乐风格上，专辑跨越克莱兹默、昆比亚、桑巴、非洲节拍及中东旋律等多种世界音乐传统，铜管类乐器在即兴段落展现出扎实的演奏功底，乐句常与节拍形成对位。整体气质轻松幽默，以装置创作传递出'音乐无需昂贵乐器'的普世理念。DIY 乐器实验与世界音乐融合的独特路径，对关注实验与世界音乐交叉领域的听众具有相当吸引力。

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio

items._genre: free jazz / Norwegian folk fusion / experimental
items._cn_summary: 这是挪威 Camilla Hole Trio 的最新专辑《Langs》，延续了前作《Eventyrferd》中跨域探索的思路，将斯堪的纳维亚民间素材与爵士即兴、模块合成器及电颤琴等实验音色并置。乐队主奏乐器为高音萨克斯，辅以低音提琴与爵士鼓配置。乐评以开篇曲《Springleik》为例展开，这首源自挪威西部传统舞蹈配乐的曲目，在三重奏框架下呈现出高度自由的互动结构：主奏旋律在萨克斯与低音提琴之间流转，鼓手则持续拓展节奏的开放空间，三人角色边界模糊，即兴成分浓厚。评论还提到卡尔曼的模块合成器与内斯海姆的电颤琴叠加录音，为传统曲调增添了色彩层次。整体来看，这张作品将挪威乡土音乐语汇置于当代爵士与即兴美学的语境中重塑，是北欧场景中民族音乐与先锋爵士融合路线的代表性新作。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — At the time, I thought Strange Little Girls was the last album where Tori Amos pursued a specific stylistic direction; just as she had previously dedicated albums to the sound of the acoustic piano or the clavichord, here she focused on the Wurlitzer (alongside her classic B�sendorfer piano), which gave the record a very special atmosphere. Yet that wasn't the only thing distinguishing the �lbum, which was dedicated to covering songs originally performed by men and giving them a feminine twist. However, rather than focusing on the personas she created for each track, I want to concentrate on the music itself; each version is distinct and received such a unique treatment, akin to applying makeup, that the song was transformed until it became unrecognizable, turning into something entirely new. This reveals the true meaning of reimagining a song."New Age", originally by The Velvet Underground, is transported to another dimension: a cold, futuristic realm, ripped without anesthesia from its quasi-hippie, Buffalo Springfield-esque setting. Tori sings with restraint at first before letting go; her voice sounds perfect alongside the album's other star, guitarist Adrian Belew. While the original held the light of morning, she imbued this version with the shadow of dusk, its diametric opposite.Belew helps make the album more challenging and progressive; his riffs complement the spirit of Tori, which was already unconventional for the time. Then there is "'97 Bonnie & Clyde", originally by rapper Eminem, though it goes without saying that the song is unrecognizable here. It is subtle and modern, yet simultaneously evokes the 1920s, featuring a drum machine that contrasts with the sound of violins and her whispered vocals.The case of "Strange Little Girls" is intriguing; for its creators, The Stranglers, it represented a move toward modernity, embracing new wave after their punk past, while Amos takes it a step further by making it postmodern. The Wurlitzer lends a futuristic air, and her committed, uninhibited vocal performance, bolstered by backing vocals, truly makes the song her own. Matt Chamberlain provides the final touch that perfects the power of this rendition.Depeche Mode's "Enjoy the Silence" is so powerful that one need not dig deep to unlock its full potential. Stripped of all its trappings, just the song itself, a piano, and a few strings, it shone like a mineral catching a ray of sunlight, glowing even from afar.She took 10cc's 1975 track "I'm Not In Love", originally warm and even contradictorily (or paradoxically) romantic, and made it icy, almost Krautrock-esque and mechanical; it features a long introduction where the beautiful original melody is recognizable only in her vocals, yet here it feels more like a threat, even though the original lyrics seemed like a confession born of denial."Rattlesnakes", a song by Lloyd Cole and the Commotions, also retains its original melody, though the tempo has been slowed down; the country, road-trip vibe remains, driven by the sound of the Rhodes piano. However, while the original's string arrangements gave it a friendly, Waterboys-esque feel, this version seems more rooted in the rural landscape of Wim Wenders' "Paris, Texas", which, at the very least, imbues it with genuine emotion."Time", by my dear Tom Waits and taken from the album Rain Dogs, remains completely unchanged; no alteration was needed, as the only shift here lay (significantly) in the vocals. Tom's voice carries powerful tones and deep emotion, tinged with melancholy in this instance, while Tori's version holds its own distinct nuances, rooted in a similarly somber quality but stemming from different sources.Neil Young and his album Harvest need no introduction; they make even those of us who aren't huge fans of country music love it!, And Tori interpreted it as if she were Garbage, with a Portishead-style trip-hop vibe, distorting, transforming, and rocking it out, much like Neil Young had transformed Bob Dylan's "All Along the Watchtower." A double tribute."I Don't Like Mondays", the iconic ballad by The Boomtown Rats (Bob Geldof's band), was a chamber-pop track featuring distinctly New Wave strings, a rich, elaborate sound, and prominent piano work. Tori captured the song's essence while performing solo on the Rhodes; she made it more direct and sincere, less explosive, and instead, something akin to an implosion."Happiness Is A Warm Gun" (originally by The Beatles, of course) features a prominent contribution from Belew, recalling his years alongside Robert Fripp, and evokes the atmosphere of his solo album Exposure, in which the guitar intermingles with audio snippets of George W. Bush; much like Fripp's record, which also incorporated overlaid audio, this concept album cemented modernity as the norm. There is plenty of room for improvisation here, and the creative flight turns progressive once again, with a psychedelic, spacey and cosmic feel.Slayer's "Raining Blood" made people headbang and stomp along to the beat... Tori's version seems to have descended into a netherworld where neither time nor physical matter exists; consequently, it feels and is perceived differently. Her piano is deep and low, it inflicts pain (were we capable of feeling it), and her voice possesses a density equal to that of the guitars in the original. If Slayer's intention was to evoke fear, this version inspires terror.We come to the final track, one by another pianist I greatly admire, Joe Jackson: "Real Men," a classic from his album Night & Day that he always performed live. The original 1982 version already featured a drum machine, keyboards, and an uptempo beat, yet it was imbued with deep emotion through Joe's performance. Consequently, Tori didn't need to alter the song's spirit; aside from performing it as a solo piano piece, an approach she took throughout the album, modifying arrangements only when necessary, she made choices that I feel were spot-on. Just as Joe is a brilliant pianist, so is she; she infused the song with her own piano sensibility, incorporating a few additional classical-style notes. And so, in a manner that feels almost sarcastic given the final track's title and the album's overarching theme, yet while remaining deeply faithful to the defiant spirit of many of the original songs, these twelve covers found a new home.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以 Wuritzer 电钢琴为核心音色，将多位男性艺人的作品彻底重构为女性视角的全新创作。从 Velvet Underground 到 Eminem、The Stranglers、Depeche Mode、10cc，每首歌被解构至仅剩骨架后重新着色——有的被推向冷峻的未来空间，有的染上二十年代的复古光泽，有的转化为冰冷的机械感宣言。Adrian Belew 的吉他棱角与 Matt Chamberlain 的鼓机节拍构成对话，Amos 的嗓音时而克制时而爆发，在低声呢喃与完全释放之间游走。专辑的核心不在翻唱本身，而在于将既有旋律拆解为完全陌生的事物，使重塑成为真正意义上的再创造，而非简单的性别反转诠释。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The trio format suits the Canterbury scene perfectly. Soft Machine immediately comes to mind, yet a jazz sensibility permeates the French group's sound, whether through the piano or the Hammond organ. As with Soft Machine, vocals are not their strong suit; during the instrumental sections of "Voici la nuit tomb�e," they also lean into a Doors-esque psychedelia.While the classic distorted keyboard sound sets the mood, Yves Hasselmann's vocals occasionally flirt with a classical style reminiscent of Supersister, until the jazz trio element takes over. Atonal passages build great suspense and a French film noir atmosphere, fittingly enough, eventually giving way to further psychedelic sections.However, in other passages, the composition is less daring, settling into a more conventional jazz style akin to that of the previous decade. "Flamenco" follows jazz-style counterpoint, adding Canterbury-esque humor in the vein of Supersister and pushing the sonic boundaries of the trio, with outstanding work from bassist Jacques-Edmond Gour�."Passo" reminded me of Friedrich Gulda's preludes, before shifting into an improvisation more in the style of Keith Jarrett. "Soleil" bears a strong resemblance to Dave Brubeck and "Blue Rondo � la Turk"; the format of short, consecutive tracks suits the trio well following the eighteen-minute suite, as immediacy and speed were Paramount, the idea being that he who strikes first strikes twice, even if they couldn't quite sustain the dramatic tension achieved by their counterparts in Moving Gelatine Plates. The surrealist element was tempered by a classic jazz sensibility that took a bit of the intensity out of the Project, though certainly not its value or quality.
items._genre: Canterbury scene / jazz-rock / progressive / psychedelic jazz
items._cn_summary: 这张1973年的法国坎特伯雷风格专辑以三重奏编制为核心，融合爵士钢琴、哈蒙德风琴与人声，试图在器乐自由与结构之间取得平衡。开场长达十八分钟的组曲以无调性段落营造悬疑与黑色电影氛围，键盘失真音色奠定基调，间或插入大门乐队式的迷幻段落。人声偶尔流露出古典歌剧倾向，随后即被爵士即兴接管。后续短曲涵盖弗拉门戈对位、超现实幽默段落以及凯斯·贾瑞特式的自由即兴，并在节奏与速度上呼应布鲁贝克的名作。整体体现出对坎特伯雷传统的深入理解，同时保持法国爵士特有的克制气质，虽在某些段落略显保守，但三重奏的张力与即兴品质仍具相当价值。

items._cn_summary: Lustmord与Lombardo合作的《The Pulse of Atoms》以一种跨越时间界限的姿态呈现，乐评指出这张专辑无法被归入任何特定流派或时期，既像去年作品，也像二十年前的产物，又或来自未来。这种去时间化的特征暗示了制作层面的深度实验——通过氛围铺陈与低频质感构建出介于暗潮、工业与电子前沿之间的声响空间。专辑似乎倾向于以声音质地而非旋律结构作为叙事手段，将Lustmord标志性的环境压迫感与Lombardo的创作语汇相融合，形成一种持续蠕动的声场。Ipecac Recordings厂牌的发行背景进一步佐证了其面向实验听众的定位，乐评试图传达的核心在于：这是一张专注于声音本体探索的概念作品，而非迎合流行审美的产物。

items.body: Hawgood has tied Folk Reels to the idea of a mobile archive, a repository for scattered works, old tapes and encounters. Live At Still Point 2026 introduces a welcome fissure into that archive. To preserve also means admitting loss and giving it an audible measure. A work that fully embraces the loss it suffered and transforms it into living matter Live at Still Point 2026 by Ian Hawgood   A live album promises to bear witness, a weighty claim, perhaps too weighty. It evokes the idea of an event fixed once and for all, destined to return unchanged with every listen. Live At Still Point 2026 favors a memory with sections erased, passages heard only by those present at Brimscombe Mill that afternoon. The recording preserves the core of Ian Hawgood’s performance, while the contributions of two laptops used for processing were never captured in the file. A tangible absence, then, which has become the defining character of the work itself. The released sound recognizes its own limits and reveals them with rare candor. For Hawgood, the concert marked his return to performing before an audience after seven years. That fact carries more weight than a line in a press release, since his artistic journey has always sought a human dimension in the act of listening. A British sound engineer, founder of Home Normal and custodian of Folk Reels, he has built an extensive catalog around care, collaboration, tape and field recordings. At Still Point, that principle reconnects with the risk of the moment and a freedom still capable of play. Twenty five minutes, a single movement. At first come rustling sounds, calls whose source is difficult to place, brief electrical flashes. They​ resemble tentative contacts taking the measure of the air. Then a deep mass expands, gathering everything happening around it. Figures from We Are But Dream are bent and pushed towards a different sense of duration. Hawgood uses SYNTRX, Buchla sequences, sounds gathered outdoors and computers running AudioMulch, instruments from different eras surrendering their names to a single current. The music grows unhurriedly and gathers body through accumulation. A melody seems about to declare itself, then immediately chooses a less determinate form. This hesitation gives the work its intensity. No backdrop inviting distraction, no contemplative postcard. Hawgood’s ambient music asks for attention in a low voice and makes perceptible the time sound requires to change its nature. From time to time, an impulse punctures the continuity, an oblique jolt roughens the balance. It happens, that is all. The performance retains a vulnerable quality, even a slight awkwardness, precious in an age obsessed with polish. Depth becomes almost physical :: In the central stretch, depth becomes almost physical. The volume rises, the fabric thickens, while the pressure avoids all monumental emphasis. Hawgood proceeds through successive degrees of proximity: one colour enters another, the drone slowly alters its light, the breathing becomes irregular. It takes time to realize that the initial landscape is already elsewhere. At the point of greatest rarefaction, the current loses substance and seems about to fade out. The music accepts this descent. From there emerge more clearly defined figures, a gentle pulse, circling scales that bring energy without breaking the spell. The ending gathers motion and a strange, purposeful serenity, as though the sound had found a way to continue after almost dispersing. Tim Diagram’s photograph translates this condition well. Trees seen from below, pale clouds, a second pattern of foliage superimposed upon the sky. The image holds two temporalities and allows them to interfere. The album likewise contains what happens and the imprint of what escapes. The material lost from the two computers compels a reconsideration of what a document can mean. The audience heard a broader version, traversed by elements that are now irretrievable; the album offers an autonomous trajectory, barer and perhaps more exposed. Fidelity lies in the gesture, its openness to chance and the human scale of what has been preserved. Hawgood has tied Folk Reels to the idea of a mobile archive, a repository for scattered works, old tapes and encounters. Live At Still Point 2026 introduces a welcome fissure into that archive. To preserve also means admitting loss and giving it an audible measure. The still point evoked by the title becomes a magnetic centre around which everything changes: intensity, distance, density, memory. This is where the album’s achievement lies. Its beauty arises from a restrained decision: to release what survived without consoling reconstruction and to entrust absence with an active role. At the end, an unusual feeling lingers. Has one listened to a concert, or to the memory that a concert produced inside a machine? The question matters more than any answer. Hawgood offers twenty five minutes freed from the pose of the celebratory live album and the smoothness of the ambient product. The sound breathes, falters, gathers strength and recedes. In that movement it carries with it the Still Point community, the apprehension of returning, the pleasure of experimentation and the part that no medium will ever be able to hold. A work that fully embraces the loss it suffered and transforms it into living matter. Live at Still Point 2026 is available on folk reels. items._genre: ambient / experimental electronic / drone / field recording
items._cn_summary: Ian Hawgood的现场录音专辑以二十五分钟的单乐章结构展开，从开场难以定位的沙沙声与短促电闪出发，逐步汇聚为深沉的音块。作品运用SYNTRX、Buchla序列、外景录音与AudioMulch实时处理，将不同时代的乐器融为一道统一的声流。旋律始终处于即将浮现又立刻消退的犹豫状态，这种迟疑构成了作品的核心张力。值得注意的是，两台用于声音处理的笔记本电脑信号未能被录音捕捉，这种有形的缺失成为作品最具辨识度的特征——声音主动承认自身的局限，并以罕见的坦率将其揭示。整张专辑延续了Hawgood围绕关怀、协作、磁带与田野录音建立的美学脉络，将环境音乐对倾听时长的要求具体化，让声音改变自身性质所需的时间变得可被感知。

items.body: Review by WizardGirl420 — I write this review in 2026 of an album I listened to extensively when it was released in 2008. Iremember listening to it nonstop for days on end. for years I couldn't listen to THE BEDLAM INGOLIATH without feeling transported in time to 2008-09. So I put it away, so I could live in thepresent.Recently I decided to pick up this album again. It still feels vital. so full of energy. At thisstage in their career the Mars Volta were firebrands of creative energy, one of the leading lightsof the 00s prog rock revival. Their well-earned Grammy win for WAX SIMULACRA, a lead single fromBedlam, was the crown to commemorate this creative peak, before they eventually declined and splitinto assorted side projects. (the followup, OCTAHEDRON, is a significant drop in quality in myopinion, which I don't think they ever got much better from. But I digress.)The album opens with a slam with "Aberinkula". The Mars Volta's trademark complex, salsa-influenceddrum patterns and highly effected guitar is a relentless blast of rocking. I love Rodriguez-Lopez'sguitar style, there's the noisiness from his experience in hardcore punk, but he's obviously verywell-versed in jazz and latin styles with a healthy dose of psychedelia. The heaviness barely letsup as the album smoothly flows into "Metatron". Everything flows together smoothly, actually; thedynamic and mood shifts between the songs feel so natural."Ilyena" is my personal favorite. Extremely catchy, and the electronic noise gives you a nice breakfrom the punk-influenced intensity that defines the album. The rest of the album follows a similarstyle of punk heaviness, electronic distortion, prog rock composition and latin rhythms. Veryunique, very catchy, very loud and very gripping.FRANCES THE MUTE and DE-LOUSED IN THE COMATORIUM might be overall better, and have probably beenmore influential on subsequent prog-minded artists. But THE BEDLAM IN GOLIATH remains a personalfavorite of mine and I think is a great piece of 2000s heavy.
items._genre: heavy prog / experimental rock / latin-influenced / psychedelic
items._cn_summary: 这张2008年的专辑被乐评人视为火星乐队的创作巅峰之作。整张作品以硬核朋克式吉他噪音为底色，融入爵士、拉丁节奏与迷幻色彩，鼓点编排复杂且充满萨尔萨舞曲式的律动。专辑内歌曲之间的衔接极为流畅，情绪与动态的转换自然而无缝。评论特别提到'Ilyena'是个人最爱，其电子噪音段落与朋克强度形成有趣的对比，在密集的声墙中提供片刻喘息。整张专辑延续了乐队前作的实验精神，将拉丁音乐传统、前卫摇滚结构与电子扭曲效果编织在一起，是2000年代前卫摇滚复兴中具有代表性的声音实验。
