items.body: Uboa releases the live album “Every Reactor Four a Friend (Live at Roadburn 2024)” through The Flenser on 22 September 2026, with a vinyl edition to follow as part of the label’s Membership Series 8 Exclusive. The three-track release is a recording of “Meltdown,” a piece Roadburn commissioned Uboa to compose for its 2024 edition. Uboa’s ‘Meltdown’ performance from Roadburn 2024 Roadburn commissioned Uboa to write two original works for its 2024 festival: “Calm Down,” a quieter piece, and its counterpart “Meltdown,” performed alongside TOomD’s “Shut Down.” “Every Reactor Four a Friend” is the live recording of “Meltdown,” captured from the mixing desk at Roadburn and later remixed and reworked, since some onboard vocal effects and microphones were missing from the available stems. The title refers to Reactor Four at Chernobyl, the reactor that melted down in the 1986 disaster. Musically, the release leans on power electronics and cut-up harsh noise, closer to the extremity of Uboa’s 2018 album “The Sky May Be” than the more intricate construction of her recent records. Uboa described the themes behind the performance directly: “It’s about embracing the overwhelm rather than shaming oneself for it. All the shame, anger and overwhelm was put in this short performance.” She added: “Sometimes it’s fine to just crash the fuck out. Sometimes it is necessary.” The album runs three tracks: “Dys,” “Do Not Comply In Advance” and “Ascension Threshold.” Every Reactor Four a Friend (Live at Roadburn 2024) by Uboa The Flenser also published a full-album stream of the performance: All Bandcamp proceeds from “Every Reactor Four a Friend” go toward covering Xandra’s gender-affirming surgery costs through 21 October 2026. About Uboa Uboa is a solo power electronics and noise project active since 2010, based in Melbourne, Australia. Early releases “Sometimes Light” (2010) and “Jouissance” (2013) were self-released before the 2018 album “The Sky May Be” arrived on the Australian label Art As Catharsis. “The Origin of My Depression” followed in 2019, initially self-released before The Flenser reissued it on vinyl after Uboa signed to the San Francisco label in February 2023. The Flenser then released the 2024 studio album “The Great Impossible Light,” featuring contributions from Blood of a Pomegranate, Otay:Onii, Charlie Looker and Haela Hunt-Hendrix of Liturgy. Uboa performed three sets at Roadburn Festival in Tilburg, Netherlands, in April 2024, including the live debut of “The Origin of My Depression” performed in full alongside the commissioned pieces “Calm Down” and “Meltdown.” “Every Reactor Four a Friend (Live at Roadburn 2024)” is the recording of that “Meltdown” performance, released through The Flenser two years on.
items._cn_summary: 这张现场专辑收录了澳大利亚噪音/极端电子艺术家Uboa于2024年Roadburn音乐节演出的三首作品，由旧金山独立厂牌The Flenser发行。作品源自音乐节委约创作的《Meltdown》，与另一首更安静的《Calm Down》构成对位。标题致敬1986年切尔诺贝利四号反应堆的熔毁事件，音乐融合强力电子与拼贴式刺耳噪音，比2018年专辑《The Sky May Be》更趋极端，回归早期粗糙质感。艺术家将羞耻、愤怒与崩溃感注入短促的现场表演，主题围绕接纳精神崩溃而非自我审判展开。由于现场部分人声效果与麦克风素材缺失，录音在混音台捕获后进行了重混与再处理。Bandcamp版收益用于资助艺术家的性别确认手术费用。

items.body: Two pizzas, a boombox, and a demo CD-R were enough to keep Michael Mayer and Wolfgang Voigt out all night. In Mayer’s recollection, their first encounter with the music of young Regensburg producer Markus Guentner began in a Cologne park. The listening session continued as they wandered through the city, playing the same three tracks over and over. Something in those recordings had altered the evening sufficiently that neither man wanted to switch them off. “We knew that we had found something outrageously beautiful and we wanted the whole world to listen,” Mayer recalls. A quarter-century later, that encounter offers a useful way into In Moll. Music associated with introspection and solitude first won over two of its most consequential listeners in the open air, among streets and other people. It could change the character of a place, and the quality of the time spent there. As the album’s 25th anniversary is celebrated this September, those possibilities remain central to its appeal. Its return through Rafael Anton Irisarri’s Black Knoll Editions on November 6, 2026 also brings a substantial restoration: the complete album will finally be available on vinyl, including the previously omitted “In Moll 4.” The photographs from around the album’s creation bring its history back to an everyday scale. There are headphones around Guentner’s neck, rows of mixer controls, a Technics T-shirt, and him as a young man sitting on a sofa with his arms folded. They place a face and familiar surroundings beside music often discussed in terms of vastness. Guentner was about twenty when In Moll appeared. Its compositional assurance can make that easy to forget. Markus Guentner around the time of In Moll’s original release. His Regensburg EP had appeared on Kompakt in 2000. “Regensburg 1” and “Pilot” followed on the inaugural Pop Ambient 2001 compilation, alongside music by Dettinger, Ulf Lohmann, Joachim Spieth, and others. The series gave a name and a shared home to an area of experimentation within the label’s wider electronic community. Melody could remain immediate even as the familiar structures of a song dissolved; repetition could carry an emotional charge without being organized around a dancefloor payoff. Kompakt’s account of Pop Ambient emphasizes pop as an attitude, connected to subculture and Pop Art. That distinction helps recover the uncertainty and excitement of the early records. Producers were investigating what happened when the machinery of club music was allowed to move at another pace. A phrase might expand until its texture became as absorbing as its tune. Bass could give weight to an otherwise suspended passage. The space surrounding a sound became part of the composition. In Moll belongs to the cultural interval those experiments opened up. In the chillout and comedown era, electronic music had acquired a life in the hours surrounding the club: the quiet room, the trip home, the morning when exhilaration gave way to more complicated feelings. Dub minimalism’s treatment of bass and empty space met a distinctly post-industrial sadness. Guentner gave that meeting an unusually intimate form, allowing warmth and unease to occupy the same stretch of music. Wolfgang Voigt’s GAS was an obvious contemporary reference point, with its dense textures and softened rhythmic presence. Guentner developed a more private expression within related territory. In his April 2002 review for Pitchfork, Mark Richardson recognized the connection while drawing attention to the album’s industrial unease and enclosed spaces. That early response is useful now: the music’s beauty has always accommodated discomfort. Its emotional proximity to post-punk is easy to understand. Solitude, urban stillness, and longing held under restraint have sustained entire bodies of work in that tradition. In Moll, whose title translates as “in minor,” gives those feelings an electronic form. The low frequencies suggest weight and distance; small melodic details offer something close enough to hold. Melancholy becomes a relationship between the individual and the space around them. You can imagine the deserted street as readily as the room overlooking it. That relationship gives the ten-minute “In Moll 3” particular significance. The album’s most popular track, selected as the anniversary edition’s second single, is an especially apt introduction to its darker emotional register. Its heavy synthesizer layers and deep echo give it a substantial, almost architectural presence. Within that scale, the melodic pull remains personal. The tension between those qualities helps explain how a piece of such duration can become the record listeners return to most readily. Ten minutes also allows a different kind of encounter with a piece of music. A feeling can occupy the foreground, recede, and become apparent again as attention shifts. For listeners drawn to coldwave’s inward concentration or dream pop’s prolonged emotional suspension, “In Moll 3” offers a natural point of entry. Its place at the centre of this anniversary campaign makes sense: it gives newcomers enough time to discover the album’s proportions, and returning listeners a reason to settle into them again. Watch the visualizer for “In Moll 3,” with music and video by Markus Guentner, below: Born in Regensburg, Germany, in 1981, Markus Guentner discovered electronic music at thirteen and secured his first weekly DJ residency while still a teenager. His listening extended across shoegaze, dream pop, indie rock, pop, ambient, and techno, giving him an appreciation for both the directness of a melody and the expressive possibilities of texture. Those interests informed a musical life rooted in his hometown, where he later co-founded the SUBLIME collective in 2006. The connection to the broader post-punk family also has a concrete history. In 2005, Guentner worked with 4AD founder Ivo Watts-Russell on The Hope Blister’s Underarms and Sideways, supplying the reworkings that formed its second disc. His version of Talk Talk’s “Such a Shame,” featuring Dana Grey, had meanwhile carried his affection for pop into a club setting through Ware Records. These projects reflect a musician whose interests could move naturally between a song’s emotional clarity and the possibilities of abstraction. Across releases for Kompakt, Ware, Warner, Sending Orbs, and Affin, Guentner has continued to move between minimal techno, beatless composition, and extended drone. Collaborations with Rafael Anton Irisarri, Julia Kent, Brock Van Wey (bvdub), Joachim Spieth, and zakè have brought other approaches into contact with his own, sustaining an exchange between musicians whose work shares an interest in depth and duration. His association with A Strangely Isolated Place began in 2012 with Talking Clouds, released through the label’s Places Series. Theia followed in 2015, beginning the loosely connected trio of albums completed by Empire and Extropy. These records gave his bass drones and slow melodic developments a larger, cosmic setting. In 2024, Kontrapunkt brought eight collaborations together, with contributors including Arovane, Abul Mogard, Benoît Pioulard, Karen Vogt, and Hollie Kenniff. Guentner’s work also extends into graphic design and cinema. His longstanding partnership with Joachim Spieth includes shaping Affin’s visual identity, while his music has featured in Drake Doremus’ Equals. That attention to the relationship between sound and image continues in the new visual presentation he has designed for In Moll. For Irisarri, the influence of In Moll reaches directly into his own beginnings. He first heard the album shortly after its 2001 release, while still discovering what he wanted to express through electronic music. “Markus showed me entirely new possibilities for what electronic music could communicate,” he recalls. His assessment of its importance to his project The Sight Below is unequivocal: “The Sight Below would not have existed without IN MOLL paving the way.” Brock Van Wey, better known as bvdub, remembers a similarly personal recognition. In his anniversary recollection, he describes hearing an unfamiliar producer articulate feelings he was struggling with far away: “it was as if that album was made to comfort me.” Their eventual friendship brought the additional pleasure of finding kindness in a musician he had admired for years. Such accounts give the word “influence” some substance. A record helped someone feel understood; that listener went on to make music of his own. Irisarri’s stewardship of the anniversary edition gives that history a particularly satisfying continuation. An artist whose possibilities were expanded by In Moll has now undertaken its new analogue remaster. The restoration of “In Moll 4” corrects a long-standing difference between the original formats: the piece was included on CD, while the vinyl edition left it out. Its first appearance on vinyl restores the seven-part sequence to the format, preserving the full span of the work. For an album so dependent on the relationship between duration, density, and release, completeness has an artistic value as well as an archival one. Guentner has also designed a new visual presentation for the edition, extending his involvement beyond the recordings themselves. The album returns with the care of its maker and of a musician it helped inspire. Richardson, looking back in the accompanying press materials, calls it “one of the finest ambient releases of the 00’s.” The strongest argument for that assessment lies in how readily the record can still enter the present. Heard in 2026, its patient pacing and emotional economy feel entirely current. Contemporary interest in slow music and environmental listening gives fresh context to choices Guentner was making twenty-five years ago. He understood how a recording could become part of a room while retaining its own complicated emotional life. In that sense, the world has gradually caught up with In Moll: more listeners have found reasons to seek the concentration and depth it has offered all along. That brings us back to Mayer and Voigt carrying a young producer’s music through Cologne. The circumstances belong to another time; the discovery remains available. Put on In Moll, give it an hour, and notice what happens to the room. In Moll (25th Anniversary Edition) is due November 6, 2026, through Black Knoll Editions (BKE025), with digital and black or white double-vinyl editions available to pre-order. Bandcamp currently lists December shipping estimates for the vinyl. “In Moll 4,” the first single, is available now. Listen below and pre-order the anniversary edition here. items.body: Infrarosso Se mi guardi, cambio forma Come fuoco nell’oscurità Infrarosso Barcelona-based duo VILLANELLE have figured out something plenty of club records forget while staring lovingly at their own machinery: rhythm gets interesting when there is a body inside it. Infrarosso, the debut single from Jessica Bellomo and Carmilla Sioux, runs on that friction. Synthesizers press forward with clean, metallic authority, the bassline prowls beneath them, and the beat keeps tightening the room until Bellomo’s voice becomes another pressure point in the arrangement. Their shared connection to rock and darker electronic music comes through two distinct histories. Bellomo is an Italo-Argentine interdisciplinary artist whose production, DJ sets, and live work span dark disco, electro, breakbeats, EBM, techno, and trance. Sioux began as a bassist in the post-punk scene before moving into electronic music as a DJ and producer, founding From Hell To Disco in 2024. VILLANELLE gives those experiences a shared form, bringing their understanding of club music into close contact with songwriting, visual presentation, and the possibilities of performing together. The writing of Infrarosso began with the instruments. Sioux developed the foundations of the bassline, and Bellomo built layers of synthesizers around it. The music took shape before the words, giving the duo a structure against which to test melodies, vocal rhythms, and different languages. That sequence helps explain the close relationship between the arrangement and the singing: the voice developed through a conversation with sounds already in motion. Traces of Pet Shop Boys appear in the chilly economy, Ladytron in the clipped sensuality, and Boy Harsher in how desire folds into sensual repetition. VILLANELLE draws from their influences without turning the song into a résumé. The bassline has enough shape to carry the track by itself, but the synth layers keep introducing new angles, giving the arrangement a strange sense of forward motion even when repetition becomes the hook. Analog warmth and digital precision meet in a track that keeps its emotional temperature unsettled. Italian gradually became the natural language for the song. Friends independently imagined the instrumental with Italian vocals, reinforcing a direction the duo were already discovering through experimentation. Its musicality, warmth, and sensual undertone suited the track’s character. As Bellomo worked through melodies, spoken-word phrases, rhythm, and rhyme, the provisional title Infrared became Infrarosso. The choice took shape in the act of singing, with the sound of the words helping determine what the song would become. Infrared suggests a presence beyond ordinary sight, something registered through heat when appearances offer little guidance. The opening line, “Se mi guardi, cambio forma”—“If you look at me, I change shape”—adds another complication: being seen can change us. Read as a statement about intimacy, it suggests the strange adjustments people make under another person’s attention, when attraction and exposure become difficult to separate. The title offers a way to sense what remains beneath those changing surfaces. The phrase Sotto la pelle, “under the skin,” became central to the duo’s conception of the track. Bellomo circles a few elemental ideas—heat, skin, darkness, disappearance—and treats language as percussion, stretching words across the beat until meaning and sensation start leaning into each other. The lyrics ask what survives between two people when the world loses light and only sensation remains. There is romance in that image, though VILLANELLE leaves enough tension in the track to imbue that romance with a bit of salt rather than sugar-sweetness. This approach also reflects the poetic dimension behind the project’s name. For Bellomo and Sioux, words participate in the rhythm and atmosphere of a composition, with repetition giving a phrase room to change emphasis. On Infrarosso, the voice works almost as another instrument, adding movement while preserving space for an emotional response. The lyric’s economy allows small shifts in delivery to carry considerable weight; the same words can feel inviting or uncertain depending on how they sit against the beat. Nicole Krämer’s video extends the same fascination with body and machine through darkness, movement, and controlled physicality. It belongs to the broader visual language VILLANELLE are developing around the music, where nocturnal elegance and bodily presence reinforce the tension within the songs. The imagery suits a track built around pressure and restraint, where sensuality comes from withholding as much as release. Read alongside the opening lyric, the camera introduces a further layer to that exchange. A song about changing under another person’s gaze becomes a performance offered to the viewer’s attention. Movement gives the rhythm a visible form, while the words continue to point toward something that cannot be understood through appearance alone. The relationship between music and image grows from that shared concern with what a body reveals and what it keeps private. Watch the official video for Infrarosso below: Live performance has helped the duo understand how these ideas reach an audience. They describe their debut at Stella Nomine as an early lesson in how strongly people could connect with the material while hearing the songs for the first time. Repetition offered listeners a point of entry, while the duo’s physical stage presence and visual interaction added another means of communication. In their account, the response in the room helped clarify what VILLANELLE could become. That experience makes the stage an essential part of the project’s development. A repeated phrase can establish familiarity within an unfamiliar song; a gesture or an exchange between performers can give its tension a visible expression. For music so concerned with perception and proximity, a live setting brings those ideas into a shared space. The audience encounters the people responsible for the sounds, and the performers discover how those sounds affect others. Released September 10, 2026, Infrarosso introduces a duo already thinking beyond one song. An album is planned for spring 2027, with further exploration of the relationship between voice, instruments, electronic production, and the body. Their debut establishes the terms with considerable assurance: post-punk’s rawness, Italo’s melodic appeal, and electronic music’s physical force all have a place in the conversation. The duo describes the intention behind Infrarosso as “music intended to be felt — somewhere beneath the skin.” Across the recording, the video, and their account of performing live, that idea takes a concrete form. A bassline becomes a framework for synthesizers; a voice finds its language inside their patterns; movement carries the song into view. By the time an audience answers, the private sensation has become something people can share. Listen to Infrarosso below and order the single, out now via From Hell To Disco, here. items.body: You said we’d never change You said we’d never fall I held on to every word I believed it all Forever is an ambitious promise to make on behalf of two people who are still changing. Romance encourages this sort of confidence, giving even the most cautious among us the vocabulary of someone who has personally inspected the future. When the relationship ends, those assurances acquire a different meaning, and the person who believed them has to wonder how much of the deception they helped along. Leipzig’s Kalte Steine turns that uncomfortable recognition into the cool, deceptively buoyant synthpop of “Love Is A Lie.” Following the social suffocation explored in “Drowning,” the single brings the question of dishonesty into a more intimate setting, where two people discover that sincerity offers little protection against making promises they cannot keep. A breathy exclamation hangs in reverb as the title refrain begins, with cool synthesizer tones underneath. Bubbly figures and bell-like notes soon brighten the arrangement, joined by a danceable drum-machine beat whose straightforward momentum gives the song its immediate pop appeal. There is an easy catchiness to these parts, each phrase leaving enough room for the next to register. The declaration that love is a lie becomes remarkably easy to sing along with. Buzzing synths and guitar tones gather beneath the first verse, while a brief metallic ripple of programmed percussion adds a small disturbance to the steady beat. The vocal sits high in the register, smooth and quietly sorrowful, carrying disappointment through its tone as much as its words. Deep bass strumming adds weight below, grounding the brighter electronics in the song’s private reckoning. The arrangement keeps moving even as the singer returns to assurances that have become difficult to hear. Initially, the lyrics give that disappointment a familiar address: “You said we’d never change / You said we’d never fall.” Every promise belongs to someone else, and the singer occupies the apparently straightforward position of having trusted the wrong person. The repeated title sounds conclusive enough to close the case. Yet the second verse quietly changes the pronouns: “I said we’d never change / I said we’d never fall.” The same words now come from the person who has been condemning them, making the earlier accusation considerably harder to sustain. “I promised you forever / Like it could be true / Oh I believed it too” supplies the song’s most revealing admission. Both people have mistaken the intensity of a feeling for evidence that it will last. Desire makes the promise persuasive to the person speaking as well as the person listening, complicating the chorus’s sweeping verdict. Through the repeated “Promises,” the post-chorus keeps returning to that shared vocabulary, setting “Words of love / Hearts on fire” beside “A web of lies / Built on desire.” What once sounded reassuring has become a reminder of how willingly both participated. When the chorus returns, melodic guitar figures add detail without crowding the hook, their economical phrasing intricate enough to reward attention and direct enough to stick. A laser-like synth accent introduces a little electronic whimsy, suggesting the beginnings of acceptance within the song’s disappointment. That small, almost playful touch suits a lyric that has gradually surrendered its claim to innocence. By the end, “Love Is A Lie” sounds like something the singer is still trying to believe, perhaps because admitting that the love was real and the promises failed is harder. Listen to Love Is A Lie on Spotify below: Love Is A Lie continues the English-language direction heard on “Crying Out” and “Drowning,” extending a catalogue that also includes “Shattered,” “Dysthymia,” “Wüste aus Beton,” and “Kinder der Nacht.” As explored in our earlier feature on Kalte Steine, the project has moved between personal fracture, urban alienation, and nocturnal escape. Here, its attention settles on the distance between what lovers mean and what they can reasonably promise. items.body: I’ll always wait for you The promise that someone will wait forever has enjoyed an excellent reputation in love songs, considering how uncomfortable it can become outside them. Patience can deepen into devotion, but it can also give obsession an alibi, allowing someone to call an inability to let go proof of a superior kind of love. London trio Black Doldrums explore that uneasy territory on Waiting, a song whose tenderness comes with the unnerving suggestion that nobody has agreed on when the waiting should come to an end. The third single from Repetition Compulsion, due November 13th, 2026, via Fuzz Club, carries a particular connection to the band’s previous album. Written around the same time as In Limerence, it extends that record’s preoccupation with longing and romantic fixation into a love song that sounds both consoling and quietly bereft. Its accompanying video takes those feelings out into the city, where a solitary attachment becomes an increasingly threatening pursuit. A deep, humming bass and the heavy thud of drums establish the song’s measured pace, while a cool, jangling guitar melody moves between high, glassy notes and lower, mournful phrases. There is something of The Chameleons in the guitar’s arcing melodies, and of The Cure in the funereal weight beneath it. Sheets of icy synthesizer widen the space around the instruments, giving the opening a peculiar calm: everything sounds composed, even as the melody suggests that something has gone terribly wrong. When Kevin Gibbard begins singing, the synthesizers settle into warmer mid-range tones, bringing a little bodily comfort to that cold room. His voice carries some of Andrew Eldritch’s solemn authority in a slightly higher register, with an exposed ache that also recalls Ian Curtis. Beneath him, the guitar takes on an increasingly Cure-like character, its clear notes ringing against the low end. Then the chorus rises into “I’ll always wait for you,” stretching the promise into a lament. The guitar’s answering jangle supplies the small, involuntary chill, the sort that travels up an arm before the mind has decided whether the feeling is pleasure or dread. For all that unease, the song began in an ordinary moment of affection. Gibbard wrote the lyrics early one morning while waiting for Sophie Landers to wake up, with the themes of their second album still close at hand. “When we were going through the finished mixes of the second album, Sophie noticed this recurring theme of limerence, which pushed ‘Waiting’ further in that direction. I liked the idea of writing about waiting for someone you love, that if you love someone enough, you’ll wait forever. I wrote all the lyrics in one go, early one morning, while I was literally waiting for Sophie to wake up. I just started jotting it down.” Landers also supplied the idea behind one of the recording’s stranger details, asking for a sound that would suggest a spirit departing its body. Gibbard found his approximation through a Mellotron, voice synthesizers, and pitch bend: “Sophie wanted something that sounded like a soul leaving someone’s body. So I played around with a Mellotron and voice synths with pitch bend to create something similar. It seemed to fit nicely because it has this really haunting sound.” That imagined departure hangs over a song devoted to staying. The warmer synthesizers offer closeness, while the guitars and spectral vocal textures suggest distance, absence, and the possibility that a promise might outlast the person it was made to. There is considerable romance in Waiting, though very little reassurance that romance will make anyone happy. The video’s darker premise took shape during a recent viewing of Taxi Driver. Landers recognized connections between the film and the band’s interest in limerence, particularly its treatment of loneliness, idealization, mental distress, and destructive fixation. Black Doldrums developed those observations into a story about an isolated, obsessive man following a woman through the city, with his sense of control destined for a nasty correction. Gibbard and Landers occupy a nocturnal world of café booths, shuttered shopfronts, graffiti-covered brickwork, and stretches of nearly empty pavement. He sits alone with a cup, writes on a loose sheet of paper, and eats in a café; she walks through the streets in a black leather jacket, occasionally looking back. The editing brings their separate movements into an uncomfortable relationship, while red-lit close-ups of her eyes interrupt the greenish darkness outside. The ordinary business of getting through a night begins to feel charged with the possibility of being watched. As the distance between them closes, the action moves into a narrow pedestrian underpass, its fluorescent lights leaving little room for either figure to disappear. Landers walks ahead while Gibbard follows, until a look back changes the balance between pursuer and pursued. The closing image gives heartbreak an abruptly physical form, making the familiar business of giving someone your heart seem like an offer best considered carefully. Watch the video for Waiting below: Gibbard and Landers formed Black Doldrums in London, initially working as a duo built around guitar, drums, and vocals before expanding into a trio. Their 2022 debut Dead Awake and 2024 follow-up In Limerence, both released through Fuzz Club, brought their early interests in psychedelia, drone, and reverb into a more concentrated gothic post-punk form. Extensive UK and European touring followed, including arena dates supporting Archive and their own headline shows. Repetition Compulsion completes the band’s interconnected “State of Mind Trilogy,” exploring the emotional patterns people carry into relationships, memory, and self-understanding. Across eleven songs, the record expands those concerns into inherited behaviour, politics, and mental wellbeing. Waiting provides a particularly intimate connection between the trilogy’s final two chapters, holding affection and fixation close enough for their resemblance to become unsettling. The album arrives November 13th, 2026, on 180-gram neon-yellow vinyl limited to 350 hand-numbered copies, 180-gram ultra-clear vinyl, and CD. Pre-order the album here. items.album: Boston’s GOSSIP COLLAR Explore Faith, Fear, and the Frailty of Flesh on Gothic Post-Punk LP “Eaten of Worms”

items.body: His curved neck bent right back to see the swan Dreading the four steps up and over to where we ran I reached the viewing point and I sit here watching and waiting But then sometimes life’s unkind Boston’s GOSSIP COLLAR makes post-punk as though somebody locked Ladytron in an abandoned theater with a deathrock band, a stack of Killing Joke records, several reels of damaged fairy-tale film, and instructions that nobody gets out until dawn. Somewhere behind the electronic throb and serrated guitar on their latest offering, the EATEN OF WORMS LP, there is also the emotional breadth of the Chameleons, a little Breeders crookedness, and that marvelous early-goth conviction on bass guitar. The band began with best friends playing and dancing in a dark Boston basement at the tail end of the pandemic, drawing together members of The Showcase Showdown, Spitzz, and Secret Hearts. They describe this incarnation as their “dark punk chapter,” which sounds about right, though “chapter” seems almost too civilized for music filled with drowning sailors, torn bodies, predatory birds, collapsing circuses, religious dread, and people standing beside freezing seas wondering precisely when existence developed such a personal vendetta. There are obvious ancestral spirits here: Xmal Deutschland, Parálisis Permanente, early Siouxsie and the Banshees, the strange congregation that gathered around the London Batcave when punk discovered it could wear theatrical makeup without surrendering its teeth. They sound less interested in reconstructing 1982 than in asking what happens when those old poisons get poured into present-day arteries. Their live pedigree adds another clue. GOSSIP COLLAR have shared stages with The March Violets, Pink Turns Blue, Rendez-Vous, Haunt Me, House of Harm, Fotocrime, and Sympathy Flowers, placing them comfortably among bands for whom darkness still needs rhythm, muscle, and enough propulsion to keep bodies moving even while the songs are busy describing spiritual ruin. Throughout the songs on EATEN OF WORMS, nature rarely provides comfort. Seas threaten to swallow people, birds wait for flesh, wolves pursue deer, plants cut skin, rain destroys, and the night contains forces that clearly have not received the memo about personal boundaries. GOSSIP COLLAR’s apocalyptic fairy tale grows out of this collision between childhood imagery and adult terror, where forests, animals, oceans, and old religious symbols have all turned slightly hostile. Edgar Froese once said, “There is no death, there is just a change of our cosmic address.” GOSSIP COLLAR sound perfectly capable of furnishing the house he moved into. Disguise My Heart opens with a saxophone-like drone, its low complaint quickly overtaken by a deep, quick-moving bassline and drums that strike with the urgent physical force of Joy Division’s Love Will Tear Us Apart. The guitars pick out a cold, melodic figure before heavier layers gather around it, giving the song a density that makes the vocal seem to travel from somewhere beyond the instruments. Witchy and windblown, the voice calls through the mix with a banshee’s sense of occasion, stretching the distance between the rhythm section’s forward charge and the solitary figure waiting beside the Northern Sea. Freezing water, aching eyes, and blood threatening to turn cold give emotional injury a bodily presence; the guitars seem to press against the skin as insistently as the memories. Even as the drums push onward, the song remains fixed on that desolate stretch of coastline. Heartbreak becomes architectural here: eventually you stop carrying it around and simply move into it. Scavengers follows with a sheet of cold guitar and an insistent bass throb, burying an unusually inviting melody several layers into the disturbance. When the arrangement briefly catches its breath, the bass leads the voice into view, exposing the sharp, declamatory cadence beneath its witchy inflections. There is an anarcho-punk edge to the delivery, a sense that these words are being hurled across a room even as the guitars make that room feel enormous. That force suits a song whose speaker lies broken, bleeding, and apparently available to whatever happens to be circling overhead. The hook keeps drawing the ear back through the commotion while memories collect like personal debris beside the body. Death may happen quickly, destruction takes its time, and the promise of resurrection supplies a final complication. Apparently even carrion birds are going to have to wait their turn. A brief arc of distortion introduces Big Top Comes Crashing Down, followed by a jagged guitar figure that rings with the blunt insistence of a tolling bell. Once the drums and bass hit, the riff acquires a crooked melodic momentum, turning its initial severity into something almost indecently catchy. Above it, the vocal echoes with a thunderous breadth, making the performance feel much larger than the cramped emotional circumstances it describes. White greasepaint goes on, the smile gets rehearsed again, and another day disappears beneath the effort of remaining presentable. That circling guitar figure becomes an apt accompaniment to the work of doing it all again tomorrow. The image of someone maintaining the same expression for ten years on Exmouth Street carries the ugly comedy of a photograph that has outlived everybody’s patience. Keep smiling hard enough and sooner or later your face becomes part of the prison. Haerisis gives the bass room to announce itself, opening with a thick, deliberate strut locked to the drumbeat. Sustained guitar tones spread above that steady march, and the clearer placement of the vocal lets its chanting insistence register more directly. The arrangement has a substantial physical weight, with dense guitar chords and more melodic lines carrying on around a groove that remains easy to follow through all the theological panic. Blood, broken bones, forbidden chalices, frozen streams, wolves, and deer crowd the lyrics, turning belief into a landscape where almost everything can injure you. The sustained tones lend those images a sense of scale, while the rhythm section keeps their violence close enough to feel. There is something particularly effective about the orderly tread beneath all this religious dread: the song advances with the certainty of a procession whose destination nobody has thought to question. On Dead Thing, a heavy wash of guitar gives way to the splash and momentum of the drums, with the opening density settling into a firm support for the melody. Another weighty riff sweeps through the arrangement, while a persistent guitar drone keeps pressure on the spaces between its movements. The vocal sounds cavernous, its thunderous resonance making each phrase seem to return from the far end of a large, inhospitable room. Those overlapping guitar textures give the song’s fascination with self-destruction considerable force. Lions are led by their manes, weapons are made, and human ingenuity eventually discovers the convenience of turning its own inventions inward. Scars become evidence and shame becomes inheritance, yet the drums maintain enough movement to make the plea for dancing feel entirely plausible. Tenderness enters through the side door wearing funeral clothes, and the rhythm section has already made room for it. Why Me? begins with eerie chimes and a low drone, suggesting an old piano being played somewhere beyond the inhabited rooms of a house. A thick bass figure gradually establishes the song’s tension, recalling the stalking movement of the Cure’s A Forest with considerably more weight behind each step. The vocal holds its heat close, sounding troubled and intimate against the spacious opening. Around the halfway point, heavier guitars enter and the arrangement settles into a cold gothic-rock groove, increasing the pressure while keeping its movements controlled. That restraint gives the lyrics’ grotesque physical imagery additional bite. Red lips, internal screaming, and organs hanging from trees turn desire into a form of captivity, while the bass continues its patient inspection. The fascination directed toward the speaker feels increasingly forensic, as though somebody has been pinned beneath a collector’s glass and asked to appreciate the compliment. The uneasy string-like tones and warbles that open Peaceful in Daylight make its title seem optimistic well before the kick drum lands. Arcs of cold guitar stretch across the entrance, then the full beat pushes the song into motion, carrying heavy riffs and a vocal whose witchy bite grows sharper against the instrumental weight. Seaweed, dense smoke, cutting thorns, broken walls, injured skin, and abandoned nests accumulate in the lyrics, filling the song with evidence that something has gone badly wrong. The arrangement gives that damaged environment a restless physical life; every forward push seems to uncover another unpleasant detail. An old-school rock guitar solo adds a flash of theatrical excess, briefly letting the instrument take over the voice’s fevered work. Daylight may make this place easier to inspect, but there is very little in the music to suggest that inspection will bring reassurance. Spelling Misery initially gives its guitar melody a clear view of the room. The figure rises and falls over a solid rhythm section, its easy memorability providing a point of reference before heavier guitars and dark vocals crowd into the arrangement. Further melodic details appear as the song progresses, with a recurring gothic-rock guitar phrase adding small complications to the surrounding force. Those returns keep the ear attached to the song even as its family portrait becomes increasingly difficult to look at. Anger lives in the blood, a father kills the fatted calf in nervous rage, and memory falters under the effort of naming what has happened. Biblical promises of shelter follow: arrows will fail, feathers will cover the vulnerable body, and fear might be held outside for another night. The returning guitar figure offers a little steadiness amid those appeals, though the heavier passages make the promised protection feel precarious. Unsafe State opens with a buzzing synthesizer pulse and cold electronic tones, briefly suggesting a turn toward synthwave before the melodic resonance of the post-punk guitars establishes its place on the record. The vocal sits more clearly in the mix, and its somber delivery makes the song’s vulnerability unusually exposed. Where other tracks enlarge their distress through dense guitars and cavernous echoes, this one allows the words to feel nearer, with the electronic repetition giving them an uneasy regularity. Eyes lose their rhythm, time becomes a dark tunnel, and the speaker digs until their nails hurt while dead souls call from somewhere nearby. The guitar melody carries that distress with a fragile clarity, giving the song an emotional directness that makes its domestic setting especially troubling. Home is supposed to provide some distance from danger; here, danger has apparently obtained a key. The closing Merchants of the Wave begins with a bassline that shifts up and down, setting a rolling motion beneath a classic post-punk guitar figure. Broader gothic-rock arcs develop around that melody, while the ghostly vocal seems suspended above the rhythm section’s steady movement. The arrangement gives the record’s returning ocean imagery a physical shape: friends venture onto dangerous seas, boats pitch, beds shake with frantic dreams, and tears become indistinguishable from salt water. The bass keeps the song moving beneath those anxious visions, its rises and falls suggesting the uncertain footing of people trying to remain upright. Prayer repeats because repetition may be the only available defense against forces too large to negotiate with. The sea that opened the album as a place of private emotional exposure becomes a shared source of fear here, carrying the possibility that somebody loved might disappear beyond reach. GOSSIP COLLAR keeps returning to bodies under pressure: freezing, bleeding, scratched, exposed, dissected, exhausted, threatened with consumption or drowning. Yet these bodies persist. They dance. They pray. They disguise themselves. They paint their faces. They get abandoned to scavengers and announce plans to rise anyway. Musically, that stubbornness comes through in the combination of deathrock abrasion and electronic precision. Imagine Ladytron discovering a box of Killing Joke singles beneath the floorboards, then recruiting the Chameleons to widen the horizon while somebody from the Breeders quietly rearranges the furniture. Beneath all the gothic architecture runs punk’s ancient belief that anxiety becomes considerably more useful once somebody gives it a bassline. That may be why GOSSIP COLLAR’s particular apocalypse remains so inviting. Civilization has collapsed, the circus tent is falling, the sea wants your body, God may or may not be answering correspondence, and several animals appear to have questionable intentions. Fine. There is still a song playing downstairs. Might as well dance before the scavengers get here. Listen to EATEN OF WORMS below and order the album, out now via Bat-Cave Productions, here. items._cn_summary: 波士顿乐队 GOSSIP COLLAR 的首张专辑《Eaten of Worms》呈现了一种在阴暗剧院中酿造的哥特后朋克。电子脉冲与锯齿状吉他交织，律动来自 Joy Division 式紧迫鼓击与深沉的贝斯线条，鼓手和贝斯手构成了整张专辑的节奏骨架。乐队并不试图精确复刻 1982 年的声音，而是将 Xmal Deutschland、Siouxsie and the Banshees 等祖先的遗产注入当代语境，开篇曲以类似萨克斯的嗡鸣开场，随后快速被低沉的贝斯动机与打击乐接管。歌词层面，整张作品构建了一个带有末世气息的童话世界，海洋、鸟类、狼群、雨夜与宗教符号都隐含敌意，童年意象与成人的恐惧相互碰撞，形成一种暗黑寓言式的叙事氛围。成员来自 The Showcase Showdown 等地下乐队，演出履历包括与 March Violets、Pink Turns Blue 同台，在黑暗场景中已积累了相当根基。

items.body: I recently wrote about an innovation currently taking place in noise rock, where noise rock bands that have embraced everything from more elaborate and thoughtful songwriting to unsettling electronic experimentation on their 2026 releases. Some that I didn’t mention have taken on a spacious, extended approach to the genre while others have embraced a dense, radical brevity. Bands across the genre have been stretching and morphing the style into previously unknown forms over the last few years, but it feels like this year has been especially fruitful in this regard. Tankerlow’s sophomore effort Slagroom can safely be added to the growing list of innovative noise rock that has been released this year, and it stands among the best.On Slagroom, Tankerlow employs a variety of sonic and dynamic approaches. Several tracks slowly unfold with a drone-like quality. There is an openness to those tracks that allows them to breathe and bloom on their own without being forced into a preconceived form by the composers. This natural pacing gives the impression that the members of Tankerlow exhibited considerable restraint, especially within a genre known for its compositional density. This restraint is most prominent toward the end of “Ergo/Ogre” when the song gets so quiet that the listener can hear the buzz of the amp underneath vocalist Guy Azulay’s unsettling, quiet moans. Yet, within that restraint is an impressive, free-wheeling aptitude for experimentation. That experimentation is prominent throughout the album, and not just with the more expansive tracks. Hammered dulcimers, pitched-down looped vocals that sound like a horn, and feedback accidentally created in the studio are all features on the groove-oriented “Formula Baby.” This combination of various compositional approaches and experimentation give each track their own character, a trait that is sadly hard to find in noise rock.What is at least partially responsible for that experimentation is the fact that the band spent over “two consistent and meticulous years in the studio,” which also explains the high quality of Slagroom’s production. Slagroom is, simply put, the best-sounding noise rock I’ve heard all year. Aspects of the album’s mix and sonic qualities oscillate between warmth and intimacy and coldness and harshness. Many of the album's sounds have an industrial quality, but they all come through the mix with analog-like warmth and clarity. Primary vocalist Azulay’s spoken-word vocals on tracks like “DIN” sound as if he is an unwell man standing right next to you on the subway, calmly detailing his mental deterioration in broken sentences. At other times, Azulay’s vocals explode into ranting and raving fury, such as during the tortured refrain in the middle and end of “Plasticine.” The opening guitars on “Ergo/Ogre” are subdued jabs, cutting into the mix like a cold butter knife. But that guitar contrasts wildly with the clanky, claustrophobic walls of chaotic distortion that envelop the listener in the song’s more climactic moments. Other aspects of the production are more subtle, such as the kick drum in “Glory Hole” that suddenly has more gain added to it during the song’s climax. According to the band, Slagroom explores “the concept of duality and the conflicts that arise from the battle of opposites,” and that notion is represented in nearly every aspect of the album. Slagroom is a rewarding but unsettling listening experience in part because the result of so many of those “battles of the opposite” is purgatory — a sense of being perpetually stuck in the gray, struggling to answer questions on identity, capitalism, and fame. But this, along with the experimentation and assiduous attention to detail, is what makes Slagroom such an intriguing listen and one of the most engaging noise rock releases this year. Of all the innovative releases put out under the noise rock banner this year, Slagroom is easily one of the best. SLAGROOM by tankerlow
items._cn_summary: Slagroom是乐队Tankerlow的第二张专辑，定位为今年最具创新性的噪音摇滚作品之一。专辑在作曲手法上展现极大克制，多首曲目以类无人机质感缓慢展开，留出大量空间让声音自然生长与绽放，如"Ergo/Ogre"尾声低至可闻放大器底噪与主唱的低吟。实验元素贯穿始终，"Formula Baby"中运用了锤击扬琴、降调循环人声模拟管乐、以及录音中偶然产生的反馈。乐队在录音室耗费两年精心打磨，混音在温暖亲密与冰冷粗粝之间游走，兼具工业质感与模拟温暖。主唱Azulay的口语化人声时而如地铁旁病人的呓语，时而爆发为癫狂的咆哮，赋予作品强烈的剧场感与不安氛围。

items.body: Label: Edition Records, 2026 Personnel - Mark Guiliana: drums, percussion, electronics, keyboards, guitar, vocals; Nicholas Semrad: keyboards; Stu Brooks: electric bass (#3), electronics (#2,4,7,8); Tim Lefebvre: electric bass (#2,4,6); Gretchen Parlato: vocals (#4,5); Marley Guiliana: vocals (#5). Mixed feelings arose from listening to Beat Music 2.0 , the synth-infused follow-up to Mark Guiliana’s Grammy-nominated album Beat Music! Beat Music! Beat Music! (Motéma, 2019). Retro and futuristic waves emerge from Guiliana’s compositions, which draw inspiration from early gaming culture and electronic music. Still, the focus here is on human connection and collaboration, as he enlists keyboardist Nicholas Semrad, bassist Tim Lefebvre, vocalist Gretchen Parlato, and Stu Brooks on electronics. The opener, “ B.ANG ”, excavates retro electronic music through glitchy synth ostinatos that march alongside the harmonic progression, along with a mix of ambient undercurrents and Gary Numan-style electro-rock energy. Although it tests the elasticity of the song’s edges, this piece failed to leave a strong impression on me. “ B.ORN ” and “ W.EST ” are also nothing special, while “ D.RUM ”, with its industrial stomp generating controlled trepidation and Parlato’s vocals highlighting the contrasting ambient-leaning passages, has a little more flair. I did feel a spark on numbers like “ P.LAY ”, whose actively propulsive drumming, together with Lefebvre’s brawny bass fluxes and pedals, is nothing short of gravity-defying, and “ B.EAT ”, whose grooving dub atmosphere morphs into club-dance territory for a while. Brooks, who infuses relevant, to-the-point electronics into the former, switches to electric bass on the latter. Also worth mentioning is “ M.OVE ”, whose danceable techno patterns reminded me of 808 State. Cross-rhythmic tides and dramatic shifts make this one a standout. Guiliana’s passion for what he does is undeniable, yet the prevailing virtues of Beat Music 2.0 come to the fore when the layers adopt a less explicit old-school electronic vibe in favor of more modernistic experimentation. Favorite Tracks: 02 - P.LAY ► 03 - B.EAT ► 07 - M.OVE

items._cn_summary: 長谷川白紙时隔两年推出的专辑以跳跃的非洲节拍开场，呈现出鲜明的模式转变。作品大量采用与现场乐队ハハ和ヘアピンズ的合作录音，其中与月ノ美兎合作的奇幻流行曲以及旋律化的摇滚曲目拓宽了可听性。更值得关注的是松丸契的萨克斯独奏与tofubeats实况录音构成的类自由爵士式breakcore作品，以及其他展现严密编曲美学的曲目，在怪异声响与结构感之间取得平衡。整张专辑的曲风跨度极大，从funky律动到抽象声响实验均有触及，将看似不相关的元素编织为统一而富有张力的整体，展现出超越既有印象的创作自由度。

items.body:
Though this recording documents the work of thirteen of Belgium's most innovative ensembles, the real star is the Park Abbey located just outside Leuven and founded in 1129. Built and maintained for the purpose of quiet meditation, the abbey hosted the musicians who used the quiet surroundings to prepare and record their unique musical imaginings. The result is a mostly instrumental collection that mines the riches of Belgian folk and world music traditions, including Romani scales,
La Pump
rhythms, and accordion-based
bal-musette
flavors.
For example, Slovenian-native R�n�lius Bikar�s searing violin opens the set with �R�fuge.� He and his self-named ensemble channel pan-European Roma history.
Meanwhile, �Poor Boy� is a Django Reinhardt-inspired swing tune by Charlotte Pelgen & Bipolar Bows. Pelgen sings in English, and with her ukulele strumming sounding very much like a tenor banjo, the tune is enlivened by Lotte Remmen�s St�phane Grappelli-like fiddle lines.
The distinctive sound of the oud announces yet another musical tradition. Blending Mediterranean with Arabic sounds, the Lebanese-Belgian singer Amber Haddad and her trio, oudist Adil Benhsain and double bassist Martijn Vanbuel, spin a beguiling musical web. According to the liner notes (translated from the Dutch), �Tawazden� is about �seeking balance and finding peace within a complex environment.� Further, �the various spaces of the abbey and their murals are the direct source of inspiration.�
The accordion is especially prominent. So too is the Western classical tradition. Sounding almost Baroque, �Sacristia Invisibilis,� is another standout for me. Here, mandolinist Andries Boone is joined by Anouk Sanczuk on octave violin (sometimes called the baritone violin, tuned an octave lower than standard) and on harpsichord Sandra Van der Gucht. They create an indescribable sound you have to hear.
Throughout, the Abbey�s stone presence looms. Aur�lie Charneux�s solo clarinet piece �L'Ape Millenaria� is about a thousand-year-old bee that haunts the abbey. �Thila,� by Enara Navaira, evokes ancient Celts with a jazzy double bass and drum kit behind throat singing and Citera (a kind of Hungarian zither).
Airboxes is a duo who mix chromatic and diatonic accordions. Their offering �Abdij 1� sounds improvised. Again from the liner notes, �they share their impressions of the timelessness of monastic life.�
Despite the wide range of styles,
The Sound of the Abbey
has a coherence, perhaps informed by the artists� shared inspiration. The record is often surprising and always soothing. Three years in the making, the ensembles were lovingly recorded and mixed by Bert Huysentruyt and mastered by Pieter De Wagter from Equus Mastering. They have rendered a warm sound using the natural reverb of ancient stone provided by the project�s silent partner.

(Interview)

Songbooks Live
(Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张合辑记录了比利时十三支创新乐团的作品，核心在于比利时鲁汶郊外始建于1129年的帕克修道院。音乐家们在静谧环境中录制，以器乐为主，融合比利时民间音乐与世界音乐元素，包括罗姆音阶、巴尔干节奏、手风琴为主的法式bal-musette风味。曲目横跨多种传统：斯洛文尼亚裔小提琴家Bikar以泛欧罗姆历史为线索；Charlotte Pelgen以班卓琴般的尤克里里演绎Django Reinhardt式摇摆；黎巴嫩裔歌手Haddad以乌德琴编织地中海与阿拉伯之声；Boone、Sanczuk与Van der Gucht以曼陀林、八度小提琴与大键琴营造巴洛克氛围；Charneux以单簧管独奏描绘千年蜜蜂；Navaira结合喉音唱法与匈牙利齐特拉。Airboxes以半音阶与全音阶手风琴即兴对话。整体在自然石质混响中呈现出修道院的永恒感，温暖、惊奇而宁静。

items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. Find the artist online. Further reading: Otava Yo - Do You Love (Review) Sofia Rei - Umbral (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑聚焦于俄乌战争中约两万乌克兰儿童被强行带往俄罗斯安置这一议题，由乌克兰-加拿大歌手Marichka发起，召集加拿大与乌克兰两地音乐人合作录制，核心编制为全女子声乐与弦乐组合，并加入班杜拉琴、钢琴与双陶笛。曲目在传统民歌与原创作品之间交替，第二首《Rusalka》以尖锐有力的方式改编自斯拉夫民间传说中的水妖鲁斯alka仪式旋律，歌词保留了传统驱邪仪式功能；而《Foreign Land》则是一首关于少女被迫远赴异乡劳作的传统歌谣，同时被赋予当代语境，映射被掳儿童的命运。整体人声表现既有温柔段落也有激烈呈现，乐评人最初不读说明文字便感受到专辑在音乐与演唱层面的扎实力量，在阅读歌词翻译后产生了情感冲击。

items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. More to hear: United States of Alchemy - Songs of Compassion (Review) Dani Jan� - Vida (Review)

items._cn_summary: Alison Cotton 的新专辑延续了她标志性的模糊质感，在民谣、前卫与宗教感之间游走。她以中提琴、手风琴、击弦古钢琴与钢琴为核心乐器，辅以鼓、贝斯与合成器，大量作品以一次性即兴录制完成，营造出穿越时间的低语氛围。歌词取材自英国自然诗人 John Clare 的诗作，配合绵延的嗡鸣铺垫。专辑核心曲目以中世纪圣咏式的开场引入，继而发展为钢琴主导的缓慢级进旋律，是专辑中最精致的段落。整张专辑是对 Cotton 已故父亲的纪念之作，丧失感渗透于多首曲目，尤其在描绘父亲最后一次造访他所钟爱的菜地的作品中，柔情溢于言表。明与暗在此交汇，作品超越类型定义，难以归入任何既有框架。

items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. Further reading: Petrona Mart�nez - Ancestras (Review) Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes - Roi De L'Agbadja Moderne 1974-1983 (Review)
items.label: Analog Africa
items._cn_summary: Analog Africa厂牌从贝宁传奇乐团Orchestre Poly-Rythmo的浩瀚曲库中精选了作曲家Antoine Dougbé在1977至1982年间创作的录音。Dougbé以拍手打出的Cavacha节奏著称，该节奏由鼓手Belobi Meridjo从火车行进韵律中提炼，后蔓延至整个中部非洲流行乐坛。作为伏都教信仰者，他对合作乐手要求严苛，最终选择与Poly-Rythmo独家合作。专辑横跨五年的录音展现了声音质感的演变：塑料质感的吉他音色、合成器的加入，与根植于七十年代的律动形成对比。古巴songo的影响在开篇曲目中尤为明显，合成器铺垫之上，闪亮的吉他与嘶嘶作响的踩镫节奏交织。康戈洛rumba元素同样贯穿始终，合成器在高潮处回旋，为整张专辑提供了丰富的听觉层次。

items.body:
I want to personally direct you to a remarkable piece of music titled "Two Views of a Prayer," composed and written by
David Dzubinski
as part of the
Prism Quartet
's new series of collaborations called
Unlocking Your Inner Composer
. If you have listened to my radio programs, you are probably familiar with the quartet's ground-breaking, genre-blurring music. If not, there's no better introduction than this.
Performed in November of 2025 at the Free Library of Philadelphia, they invited vocalist
Ursula Rucker
, percussionist
Tyshawn Sorey
, and violinist
Carlos Santiago
to collaborate on the arrangement and performance of Dzubinski's composition. It travels from raw to lyrical and back in the course of just under 4 minutes, with both finesse and energy. - Cliff Furnald, editor

items._cn_summary: Prism萨克斯四重奏发起名为"释放你的内在作曲家"的合作系列，邀请作曲家David Dzubinski创作了《Two Views of a Prayer》。作品于2025年11月在费城自由图书馆首演，合作者包括人声表演者Ursula Rucker、打击乐手Tyshawn Sorey以及小提琴手Carlos Santiago，共同参与编曲与演奏。这是一首不到四分钟的短篇作品，素材从粗粝的质地向抒情性流动，最终回归原点。评论特别提及四重奏以跨越流派边界的演奏著称，本曲作为其合作系列的开篇，展现了当代古典乐器配置与爵士即兴、人声文本以及自由打击乐之间的高密度对话。整体属于学院派作曲思维主导的跨界合作实验，演奏技巧与结构设计均有较高完成度。

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由瑞典小提琴手与两位挪威乐手组成的跨国三重奏呈现，取材自斯堪的纳维亚传统舞曲，却以极度室内乐化的方式重新诠释。三人并非为舞蹈伴奏，而是将旋律拆解、拼贴，在小提琴、竖笛、萨克斯与鼓的交织中探索音乐被遮蔽的深层意涵。评论指出这种处理方式与易卜生戏剧中表面欢愉下潜伏暗流的修辞相似，首曲选自挪威塞特斯达尔的「Fossgrimen」传说小调，暗指小提琴与魔鬼仪式的历史关联。作品在文本化伴奏、不协和音色与静默留白中展现强烈实验意图，将民间舞曲的神秘面纱层层揭开。

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.
