items._cn_summary: 古巴钢琴家 Omar Sosa 在意大利 Fazioli 钢琴厅完成了长达两小时的即兴独奏录音，后期叠加人声采样、打击乐、循环音段、田野录音与环境声效，构筑出多层次的声响空间。专辑诞生于疫情封锁与个人生活转折期，艺术家强调直觉优先、首次录制即定稿的创作哲学，拒绝被风格标签与流媒体算法定义。音乐融汇爵士、拉丁古典与冥想氛围，呈现沉思冥想式的音乐探索路径。文中穿插艺术家本人关于创造力、传统延续与精神自由的直接引述，篇幅在结尾处戛然而止，未能完整覆盖所有曲目听感。

items.body: Editor's note: When this set of recordings came to me, I was at a loss as to how to share it. It's not music, in any traditional sense (although there is some freestyle rapping), and a 'review' of such an artifact of reality seems superfluous to the content. Instead, I asked sound recordist Ian Brennan if I could simply use his own brief commentary and the recordings he made on the street in Chicago. Twenty-five people afflicted by gun violence participated, many from the very block we�d setup on. Many neighbors were pulled-in spontaneously. Almost every one in the community had been impacted by violence somehow� both on the receiving and the inflicting end, and many both. One woman had just come from a memorial service, another was on her way. That�s how far-reaching the violence. Almost no one went untouched. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors By chance, we convened on the day that Trump ordered the deployment of the National Guard to the city. The recording took place on the front porch of the leader's ninety-four-year-old grandmother's house�right in the heart of the ��hood,� beneath the Midway Airport�s landing path. A pair of stray pitfalls stalked the block. But the grandmother warned not of gunshots, but the mosquitoes in her yard. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors We were in a section of town that one man defined as �the forgotten parts.� Just a short jaunt from the designer clothes shops and posh hotels of the city�s Magnificent Mile, the Southside spawned such legendary Blues artists as Muddy Waters, Willie Dixon, and Howlin� Wolf. Jazz musicians like Lionel Hampton and even Benny Goodman, hailed from nearby. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors The participants ranged in age from seventeen to sixty-seven, but the pattern held true. The person who�d asserted �you�ll really want to hear my story,� was the least compelling. The reluctant, the most moving. One elder�s tough facade broke down as she shared how she�d lost both her sons. She tearfully apologized, �I�m sorry. I�m sorry. I�m sorry.� But she had nothing to be sorry for. Society is the one that owes the apology� for the staggering statistical inequities of which no reasonable defense can be made. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors Editor's note: The full set of recordings are available on Bandcamp. Any profits from this project will be donated to Cure Violence Global , who states that their mission is "advancing an evidence-based health approach to end violence globally." When I asked him about the background sounds, producer Ian Brennan added, "No music is added. It�s all sounds from the source environment. I also ran loops/drones on a different track in the background as they spoke, and when they ended up being incidentally/somewhat magically/eerily synchronous, that is what was used for a few pieces with 'accompaniment' like some of the rap freestyles."
items._genre: field recording / spoken word / sound documentary / experimental
items._cn_summary: 这是一张以田野录音与口述为核心的音频文献，并非传统意义上的音乐作品。制作人Ian Brennan在芝加哥南区的街头搭建临时录音环境，邀请二十五位遭受枪支暴力影响的居民直接讲述亲身经历，参与者年龄跨度从十七岁到六十七岁。录音地点位于一位九十四岁祖母家门前，正处于中途机场降落航道之下，环境噪音与参与者陈述共同构成作品内容。作品中几乎无人工配乐，仅有少量即兴说唱，所有声音均来自现场。项目收益将捐赠给以公共卫生方法遏制暴力的国际组织。这张作品的价值在于将声音作为社会证言的载体，以声音民族志的方式记录被主流叙事忽略的社区经验，对关注声音艺术与社会田野音频交叉领域的听众具有参考意义。

items.body: “The devil is busy” is what churchgoers say when trouble arrives, and Seun Kuti & Egypt 80 take the phrase, as “Devil Just Busy”, and point it at the darkness closing over contemporary society. Seun turns the preachers’ own words back on them: on the title track and first single of his upcoming album Na Dem, he already listed reverends, bishops, pastors and imams among the “winch men” he wants saving from, and his father Fela Kuti went after the same pulpits on “Shuffering and Shmiling” in 1978. “DJB” gives the phrase seven minutes of dark, mid-tempo afrobeat, laid down by two drummers, Mario Orsinet and Femi Koleoso, and two bassists, Kunle Justice and Gbeke Ojutiku. Seun sings and plays saxophone on top, with two trumpets and four more saxophones building the horn arrangements around him. Koleoso, who leads Ezra Collective, also produced the track, as he did the whole of Na Dem. Na Dem arrives on 6 November via Django Music, eight days before Fela becomes the first African solo artist inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. Seun, who inherited Egypt 80 at 14 when his father died in 1997, will be in Los Angeles to represent him at the ceremony, five weeks after the band play the city’s Regent Theater on 9 October. That date sits in a US run that also takes in Belly Up Tavern in Solana Beach on 7 October, FORM Arcosanti in Arizona and Webster Hall in New York on 14 October. Listen to “DJB” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Seun Kuti & Egypt80 – DJB appeared first on Rhythm Passport.
items._cn_summary: Seun Kuti与埃及80乐队的新单曲延续了Fela Kuti开创的非洲节奏传统，七分钟的中速 afrobeat 由双鼓手与双贝斯手构建复合律动底层，萨克斯、小号与多支萨克斯编织厚重的铜管编排。歌词将教堂信众的俗语转化为社会批评的武器，矛头指向宗教领袖与现代社会的阴暗面。专辑由Ezra Collective乐队领袖Femi Koleoso担任制作人，将传统非洲节奏语汇与现代制作手法结合。专辑即将在11月发行，同期Fela Kuti将成为首位入选摇滚名人堂的非洲独唱艺术家。这张作品在传统 afrobeat 框架内注入政治自觉与家族传承，是非洲音乐传统在当代语境下的延续与发声。

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — A reunion, of sorts, in effect as all participants in this studio product had played with Jack in former bands; The Graham Bond Quartet (Bruce & McLaughlin), The Graham Bond Organization (Bruce & Heckstall-Smith), and Jack's previous album, Songs for a Tailor (with Hiseman). (Hiseman and Heckstall-Smith had, of course, been playing for a couple years together in David Greenslade's Colosseum--three albums worth.)1. "Over The Cliff" (2:56) a quick riff from Dick Heckstall-Smith's tenor sax launches bassist Jack Bruce and drummer Jon Hiseman into a rapid-paced expression of fairly straightforward Hard Bop Jazz. There is little to no input from John McLaughlin's guitar but Dick, Jack, and Jon are more than up for the trio presentation. Interesting and respected but this is not really my preferred type of music. (8.875/10)2. "Statues" (7:35) more blues-based Hard Bop Jazz from Dick, Jack, and Jon in which the trio dance around one another in tight and attentive circles, each playing their own consistent melody lines--Dick even going for the two-saxes in the mouth at the same time trick a couple times. In the fifth minute there is a cease and desist order so that Jack can bow his bass a bit, but then Jon rejoins with meagre little input from Dick (and, interestingly, none from John McLaughlin) before Jack steps back to let Jon have the spotlight a couple of times before the recapitulation of the opening themes over the final 35 seconds. Fine musicianship. (13.5/15)3. "Sam Enchanted Dick" - medley (7:28) bass and electric guitar recite the song's main melodies over Jon's drums for the first 30+ seconds before John is loosed with his distorted tone to solo for about a minute. Then it's Jack's turn in the third minute. John's chord accents are all I can pay attention to (for I am a HUGE fan of John's fascinating "rhythm guitar" choices). At 3:37 we hear the first squirts of Dick's, tenor sax--which leads, of course, to an extended solo for him (and yet my ears still find themselves paying attention to John's caustic chord interjections). Double saxes for a bit in the seventh minute before Dick's play on "Sweet Georgia Brown" lead to the song's finish. (13.5/15) a. "Sam Sack" b. "Rill's Thrills"4. "Born To Be Blue" (4:26) a gorgeous ballad with very sensitive performances from all four players. There is enough space in the soundscape of this song that I can very much appreciate the skills and creativity of each individual musician--which I need from time to time in order to better understand and value the musics I'm being exposed to. (9/10)5. "HCKHH Blues" (8:59) there is an auspicious threat of power and havoc in this song's music from its very opening. Despite Jack and John's pulling tendency to want to drift over into the Louisiana Bayous, Dick and Jon do a great job in keeping the spirit firmly anchored in less Southern traditions, more in the urban forms of expression. Finally pusuaded, John and Jack swing over to join Dick and John in their Coltrane-like explorations. (18.125/20)6. "Ballad For Arthur" (7:42) pensive bass notes are embellished by delicate cymbal and snare play while Dick explores his own melody ideas. There is enough focus in Dick's playing that Jack and Jon both feel empowered to let their own playing go a bit into the realms of improvisational freedom--until, that is, John feels inspired to join in (around 1:50). Thereafter John's "commanding presence" effects a stoppage from Jon (no drums or cymbal sound for over a minute!) while Dick tries to figure out how to play background accompanist role to John's spacial musings. With Jon's boisterous Jack DeJohnette-like return in the fifth minute, we find the other three suddenly inspired to become quite a bit more dynamic: each flying off in their own directions while somehow it all still manages to make sense from a collective view. With a minute left to go there is a sudden buildup and burst into controlled chaos before everybody backs out, spent. While I still don't "like" this kind of music, I understand anad appreciate the discipline and skill required to make it happen--to make it work. (13.5/15)7. "Things We Like" (3:38) another this time more targeted and speedy foray into the reactive/responsive side of Jazz' free jazz movement. There is a playfulness to this one that makes it a bit more amusing and, thus, enjoyable. (8.875/10)Total Time 48:04Despite the presence (and influence) of metamorphosizing guitarist John McLaughlin on four of the album's seven songs, the rest of the band on this album (Bruce, Hiseman, and Heckstall-Smith) are all playing Jazz, standard, blues-based Jazz albeit at times what we've come to call their own versions of "free jazz." John is the only one pushing boundaries, injecting non-standard sounds, riffs, and epithets. One might also argue that Dick Heckstall-Smith is pushing for more free jazz representation. Were I more of fan of straight Jazz (I'm trying, folks!) I might like this album more. As it stands, I feel hard-pressed to even consider this "Jazz-Rock Fusion" much less call it such.B+/4.5 stars; while Jazz afficionadoes might consider this a minor masterpiece of Jazz (or even Jazz-Rock Fusion), would call this a near-masterpiece and not a true representative of Jazz-Rock Fusion; to my mind Things We Like has got far more of the fire and focus of pure Jazz than it does of Fusion or progressive rock.

items._cn_summary: 这是一张1970年的爵士录音室专辑，参与者多为Jack Bruce此前乐队中的旧识，包括Dick Heckstall-Smith的次中音萨克斯、Jon Hiseman的鼓以及John McLaughlin的吉他。专辑以硬波普爵士为底色，兼顾蓝调元素与自由即兴片段。曲目多为三或四重奏编制，节奏紧凑，萨克斯与贝斯形成主导对话，吉他音色粗粝刺耳，常以节奏性切分和弦穿插于萨克斯独奏之间。部分曲目留出较大空间供乐手展现个人技巧，如慢板抒情曲中各乐器的细腻互动。整体偏向传统爵士范畴内的即兴演奏，虽有融合元素，但实验性与前卫性有限。评论文字本身因被截断导致信息不完整，无法全面评估后段内容。

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Early (First Wave) Jazz-Rock from Poland. This band's debut, we find them experimenting with blending several styles including Blues-Rock, Psychedelia, Procol Harum-like prog, orchestra-enriched lounge music, and more. The album was released in 1971 by Polskie Nagrania Muza.1. "Sen (A Dream)" (3:17) what feels like an ANTHONY PHILLIPS guitar piece opens this for the first 1:07 before a pause unleashes a bouncing organ chord, funky bass line, and Michael Giles-like drumming with simplistic guitar riffs over the top to announce the presence of melody. In the final 30 seconds there is this all out burst of WHO-like energy being expressed/expelled by all of the band members--which then seems to bleed/lead into the SANTANA-like frenzy that is the next song. A three-part suite in three minutes! Wow! (9.333/10)2. "Kuszenie (Temptation)" (3:29) the SANTANA-like percussion-driven full-band jam that features everybody flying at full speed. Maciej Gluszkiewicz' organ impresses as do the performances of all of the quartet members. (9.25/10)3. "Nerwy Miasta (The Nerves Of Cities)" (3:31) a slowed down PROCOL HARUM-like sound palette that comes off sounding like something from a Blues-Rock band like anything lead by vocalist ALEX LIGERTWOOD, Billy Gibbons, or 21st Century Polish band LIZARD. At the very end the band do a quick shift into high gear for minute of rousing organ-led instrumental fun to finish things off. (8.875/10)4. "Senne Wędr'wki (Wandering Dreams)" (3:52) orchestra-supported blues rock! Interesting! Quite like the sound of PROCOL HARUM. Nice imagination! (9/10)5. "Taniec Wariatki (The Madwoman's Dance)" (2:02) rock-infused theatric cabaret music (almost musique concr'te) with interesting call-and-response playfulness between the instrumentalists. Quite creative. (4.625/5)6. "Taniec Czterech (The Four Men's Dance)" (1:37) fun/funny open air, city green music by the local marching band. Nice drumming. (4.375/5)7. "Na Przek'r (Against Everything)" (2:16) opens like some folk rock from one of the Summer of Love's outdoor music festivals--with vocals (DON BREWER-like lead with Gospel church choir backing), like a. moralistic hippy musical. (4.625/5)8. "Nasze Myśli (Thoughts)" (5:10) pensive four chord progression arpeggiated by guitar with organ, drums, and bass backing while lead singer croons like a South American folk singer singing through the city center's public address system (or else LIZARD's Damian Bydliński). The very pleasant and comforting song contains a somewhat-spirited organ solo but is really just more of a nice ballad. Interesting vocal weave at the finish. Reminds me of 1990s QUIDAM. (9/10)9. "Mrowisko (The Hive)" (4:15) unusual opening with drums and organ playing cat-and-mouse-in-the-mirror for the first 35 seconds. Then a pause opens the door for a classical guitar and intermittent bombastic "symphonic" bursts of accompaniment and antiphonal response--something that gets drawn out for a minute, stumbling and fumbling, until finally fully developed at the three-minute mark. From there we get a minute of song with singing. Weird. (So like the 21st Century music of Polish band LIZARD). Yet interesting. And creative. (9/10)10. "Pejzaż Z Pustych Ram (Landscape Of Empty Frames)" (4:31) gentle electric guitar musings accompanied by responsive ghost-vocalese open this before a fully-meted song presents itself at 1:10. Singer Marek Alaszewski sounds like Jacques Brel during the delicate verse, but then things amp up for the chorus, Marek switching voice tones to something more RPI like as choir vocals chase him around like a church choir. Nice bass work from Roman Pawelski as the band and vocalists sustain the chorus intensity from here to the song's end. Very nice: emotional. (9/10)11. "Taniec Głodnego (The Starvelling's Dance)" (2:24) PROCOL HARUM palette and slow militaristic pace as organ swirls, drum and bass keep funereal time, and wooden flute (recorder) presents and carries the lead over the top. The opening motif switches into something more dance-oriented at 1:38 as Roman shifts to a walking bass line. Sounds like a wonderful night for a Moondance (Van Morrison)! Nice! (4.5/5)12. "Epidemia Euforii (Epidemic Euphory)" (3:46) not sure what is meant by this song's title, but the music feels more derivative of a combination of early British Rock and the U.S.'s Beatnik styles. By the time the band really kicks into full gear we're presented something that sounds more like Steve Winwood's first band, The Spencer Davis Group, as well as, at the percussion end, like The Chicago Transit Authority (with, of course, the Damian Bydliński lead vocal voice). (8.875/10)13. "Sen (A Dream)" (1:49) all four members of the rock combo are here represented with Marek dusting off his recorder again to muse over the gentle/calming nature-backed music. (4.375/5)Total time 41:59A very creative band of proficient musicians who create an unusual but very pleasing style of progressive rock: their songs are either isolated vignettes of imagination or conglomerations of such all smashed together. The bottom line is: that it works! I especially like the interesting use of choral backing vocals and full-spectrum and active percussion tracks.A-/4.5 stars; a collection of what feels like experimental and highly-idiosyncratic musical ideas coming from a very creative and skilled quartet of young musicians that results in a minor masterpiece of early progressive rock music. (There is little or no Jazz much less Jazz-Rock Fusion here).

items.body: Review by Thomas1969 — Every time Steven Wilson releases a new album, I think: "Wow, is it that time again?" It also occurs to me that I rarely revisit the albums released after *Hand. Cannot. Erase.* (2015). While every album since then has certainly contained good songs, none have gripped me the way the dark *Grace for Drowning* (2011), *The Raven That Refused to Sing (And Other Stories)* (2013), and the aforementioned album did.What I've missed since then is a certain emotional depth in the music, as well as that "moody" side. Fortunately, we hear that moody side return in the advance track "Requiem for a Village," taken from the album of the same name due out in November. The album cover certainly looks promising. But what about the content?the music itself? "Requiem for a Village" is vintage Wilson: a moody opening, an enigmatic progression, a guitar eruption three-quarters of the way through, busy drumming, and?this is where the real tension lies for me?the quieter passages and mysterious vocals (Wilson is singing more beautifully than ever) at the beginning and end, accompanied by evocative keyboard sounds.Of course, there is a full band behind Steven Wilson?it could easily be called the Steven Wilson Band. Who makes up the band as of 2026? Lead vocals, bass guitar, guitar, Mellotron, keyboards, percussion, piano, oboe, mixing engineer, lyre, producer: Steven WilsonGuitar, backing vocals, synthesizer, Mellotron, co-producer, lyre: Randy McStineDrums: Russell HolzmanSo, it is very much a Steven Wilson affair, but Randy McStine and?most certainly?the new drummer Russell Holzman deserve special mention. They play skillfully?you have to hand it to them?but does it truly *connect*? Does it move me? Richard Barbieri moved me with every keystroke; of that, I remain absolutely certain. I am also left with a nagging feeling?since a new The Pineapple Thief album is coming out next month as well?of whether I am looking forward more to *that* album (featuring Gavin Harrison on drums) or to the new Steven Wilson release. You might say: you still miss Porcupine Tree. That's true. You never really get over that. But what I miss most is the emotional depth found in Porcupine Tree's music. Since *Hand. Cannot. Erase.*, no full Steven Wilson album has truly moved me in the same way. That could change. It might... You probably grasp my point. My ambivalence.A bit of a mixed bag, then, this sprawling track?clocking in at 7 minutes and 56 seconds.

items._cn_summary: 评论者审视Steven Wilson新专辑同名先行曲《Requiem for a Village》，认为这首七分五十六秒的曲目重现了早期Wilson作品中忧郁、深邃的情感氛围。乐曲以低沉的开场展开，神秘的人声与键盘铺垫张力，中段爆发出吉他强烈段落，鼓手Russell Holzman与Randy McStine的演奏技巧扎实。评论者对比了前后两个时期的Wilson作品，对2015年《Hand. Cannot. Erase.》之后的专辑始终缺乏真正的情感共鸣而感到矛盾，对新阵容的化学反应存疑，同时坦承对Porcupine Tree时期那种深沉情绪的怀念。整体而言，这是一次对艺术家创作状态与乐队化学反应的诚实反思。

items.body: Strikkland are easy to misread if you mistake humour for distance. Henrik Johansson can deliver brutal lyrics while smiling, appear in a red feather boa, play with national flags or deliberately puncture the visual severity traditionally associated with EBM, but none of that suggests embarrassment about the genre. Quite the opposite. The joke works because the attachment underneath it is genuine. They are not standing outside EBM making fun of its conventions; they know those conventions intimately enough to interfere with them. I first saw the Gothenburg duo at E-Only in 2024 and again this year on the much larger Waldbühne at Nocturnal Culture Night. At NCN, something became particularly clear: humour had stopped feeling like something happening around the songs and had become part of Strikkland’s performance language itself. Hard electronic structures, Henrik’s forceful delivery and the physical directness of EBM remained intact, while gestures, costumes and irony continually destabilised the expectation that seriousness must look solemn. Their second album, “Hommage”, makes that tension especially interesting. It openly acknowledges the music that formed Henrik and Henric, while its production deliberately returns to hardware, physical studio equipment and recording practices associated with an earlier era. Yet Strikkland have little interest in turning EBM into heritage preservation. For them, tradition is useful precisely when it can still be disturbed. We spoke about growing into a band after fifty, refusing genre uniforms, why limitation can generate creativity, the ethics of AI, the strange authority of old symbols, and what happens when two people who take EBM very seriously refuse to behave as though seriousness requires a permanent scowl. Strikkland interview Karo: I first saw you at E-Only in 2024 and then again on the much larger Waldbühne at NCN this year. What struck me at NCN was how much more clearly humour had become part of the performance language itself. When did you realise that humour could be structural to Strikkland rather than merely something happening between songs? Henrik: We have always had humour as an important element of what Strikkland is all about. We started the band on impulse and as a fun thing to do. The lyrics are often conjured up at the same time as we are in the studio creating new songs. My texts often tend to drift towards dark stories about space, death, fantasy and the absurd. The humour you get from seeing the band live is something we have developed throughout all the time we have been on stage. We have fun, and that creates what we deliver. Henric: We realised early on that two old geezers would only look ridiculous if we tried to act tougher or darker than we actually are. Besides, there are plenty of bands already biting heads off chickens or dressing up in full combat gear on stage. It has all been done before, and it really didn’t seem like an option for us. Our appearance and the way we behave also evolved from criticism in Sweden after our first live shows in the early days: “Their music is half-decent, but they aren’t a real EBM band because they don’t look or behave like one.” We kind of turned that against the critics, embraced it even more and made it our thing. Karo: At NCN you told me that when you started the band, already approaching your fifties, you briefly considered becoming the “gothiest” band possible before deciding that pretending to be something you were not would be ridiculous. Did starting Strikkland later in life actually give you a kind of freedom younger bands sometimes lack, because you had less need to prove that you belonged? Henrik: Absolutely! Also, later in life you have so many more musical influences to choose from and try to implement into your own songs. Starting a band later in life also means you can afford to have a band and go places to play live without starving and sleeping in the car on the way there. We are doing something today that you thought impossible when you were young. Henric: Being close to 50 when you start a band certainly provides more freedom. Our ambition was never to release records or perform live, but when possibilities opened up, we jumped for it. Speaking for myself, I got a chance to do what I wanted to do in my teens but never got the chance to do. At 50, you aren’t as afraid of criticism or about what others might think as you are at 16 or 17. That helped a lot. Karo: EBM has accumulated a very strict visual and behavioural vocabulary: severity, discipline, confrontation, often a certain cultivated lack of humour. You clearly love the genre, but you also interfere with those conventions constantly. Which parts of EBM do you take completely seriously, and which parts do you think deserve to be laughed at? Henrik: We never laugh at EBM, but we think we can involve irony and humour in the genre and have a laugh at certain aspects of life. Humour and art are always found in the contrasts. I mostly write quite dark lyrics, but we present them with a lot of smiles, humour and dance. Henric: EBM has been a huge part of my life since the 1980s, so it is something I take very seriously. I do laugh at some of the rigidity coming from certain corners of the fanbase, though. Come on, loosen up and dance while you still can. Have fun. At least laugh a little. There are enough bitter middle-aged men in the world, and I don’t want to become one of them. Karo: That is also why “Hommage” interests me. It is explicitly a tribute to the music that formed you, but homage can easily become imitation. How do you honour an artistic language without treating it as something that should remain frozen in the period when you first discovered it? Henrik: The tribute to the EBM bands we grew up with is always there when we make music. In “Hommage”, it is in the basslines, the sounds, the technology and the artwork. I am a curious person, so I constantly look for new music and new bands to listen to. The EBM genre, and Strikkland, keep finding new ways without letting go of the legacy of the bands of the 80s. Henric: Apart from a handful of gems from bands like Kraftwerk, DAF, Nitzer Ebb, Front 242 and a few others which can’t be topped, EBM and electronic music have evolved a lot. In my playlists there are rarely any songs older than two or three years. You can still hear where it is coming from, but it has evolved. If we stick to what we grew up with, there would be stagnation and the genre would surely die out. But thanks to artists like SIIE, Emmon, Plastikstrom and many others, it is still interesting. So I would rather risk going outside the standard formula and at least try to contribute to keeping EBM alive, both musically and visually. Karo: You made “Hommage” deliberately with classic studio equipment, hardware synthesizers and drum machines, and you were very explicit about not using AI. Is that primarily an ethical position, an aesthetic one, or did you simply want the limitations of those tools to become part of the composition? Henric: AI has no place in art. Full stop. For both creative and ethical reasons. When it comes to using hardware versus working “in the box”, it is purely a workflow decision. The tactility of turning knobs and pushing buttons works better for me than using plugins. We are also privileged enough to get to work together with Hans Olsson at Svenska Grammofonstudion in Gothenburg, which is both a studio and a “synthesizer museum”. It would be stupid not to use all of those classic machines if you can. Our first album, “Bodypop”, was mixed there on an SSL 4000E console, so when we got the chance to mix “Hommage” at Hansa in Berlin on their SSL console, of course we took the plunge. And of course we did some additional recordings there as well. I mean, who could resist playing the very same Steinway grand piano that Martin Gore posed in his jocks next to? Karo: There is an interesting contradiction there: Strikkland describe themselves as expanding the borders of EBM, yet “Hommage” deliberately looks backwards in terms of production practice. Can technological limitation actually be more progressive than unlimited technological possibility? Henrik: Well, maybe in a way every EBM band today is expanding the borders of EBM? To stay in the genre, you have to remain within the frame agreed upon, regardless of what technology you use. But it gets more interesting if you drift away towards the border and sometimes cross it, bringing in other influences and expressions. That’s the way music has always evolved. Henric: For me, limitation sparks creativity. There is a certain number of available channels on a physical mixing console. On a computer, you can have hundreds. There are also limitations to hardware synthesizers and effects, and all of this forces me to be creative. As mentioned before, this is a workflow that suits me. With that said, most of our songs start out “in the box” because it is convenient. Karo: Henric writes the music and programming while Henrik handles vocals and lyrics. With such a clear division, where does the personality of a Strikkland song emerge? Does the music arrive with a character already inside it, or can the vocal idea fundamentally alter what Henric thought he had written? Henrik: Often we start with a bassline that Henric has created and then build it together from that point. I get inspiration for the lyrics and write them at the same time as Henric starts to develop the music. When both of us feel ready, we fuse it all together. This is a fast process, so we are very much in line with what kind of music we want to produce. Henric: Let’s put it this way: when Henrik enters the studio, I might have 20 loops that I have worked on for six months, with basslines, drums and maybe a melody ready. If Henrik says, “Great! But can we change this or that?”, that loop goes into the bin. But if he stops, shuts up and starts to write text immediately, I know it is a keeper. Then we combine that idea into a draft by making a rough arrangement, tweaking the text, tweaking the music and finally recording it. When we have enough tracks for an album, we take it to Hans and re-record everything. So, to answer your question, the music inspires the vocals and the vocals give direction to the final piece of music. Neither would be the same without the other. Karo: At NCN, Henrik changed clothes, exaggerated gestures and played with Swedish and German symbols and declarations of friendship. In a genre that has historically borrowed heavily from militarised imagery, does humour give you a way to use those symbols without allowing them to retain all of their old authority? Henrik: When I go to see a band live, I want to be entertained. When I am on stage, I want to entertain and have a good time! To joke around and interact with the audience and get a warm response elates me. I love the contrast of delivering hard-hitting music and brutal lyrics with a smile on my face and prancing around with a red feather boa. So yes, it is absolutely a way to deflate the power of symbols of power. Henric: Personally, I think it is important to reclaim symbols like national flags from fascists and extremists and use them in a positive way. We don’t hide behind humour and irony, but instead use them as tools for communication. Our message is clear. We don’t accept fascists, Nazis or totalitarian regimes, we support Ukraine’s fight for freedom and we advocate free speech. But maybe we have chosen a “lighter approach” to convey this than other bands, mainly because the darker image doesn’t suit us on a personal level. Karo: What I particularly liked was that none of this reduced the concert to parody because the musical foundation remained genuinely hard. Do you consciously protect that balance, making sure the joke never becomes an excuse for musical weakness? Henrik: When we make our music, we never implement humour to start with. Okay, some lyrics are rather absurd and some sound effects we add for fun, but we want our music to be serious and taken seriously. It is mostly when we play live that we joke around. Henric: Some people have clearly written us off as a parody act. No question about that! But either they haven’t seen us perform live or they haven’t understood what we are doing. Irony is a tough nut to crack for some, and others lack humour. One thing is certain, though. We would never release or perform anything that we ourselves thought was weak, and we put a lot of work into our music. Karo: You worked with Hans Olsson at Svenska Grammofonstudion and Hansa Studios on “Hommage”. Did working in spaces carrying so much recording history make you more conscious of tradition, or was the important thing precisely to forget the mythology once you were actually inside the studio? Henric: It took a while for it to sink in once we were at Hansa. We were actually sitting at the same mixing console that was used to make some of the greatest albums of my youth?! Insane! But once that feeling disappeared, it was just another day in the studio and we did our thing together with Hans. Henrik: Hans Olsson suggested mixing the album at Hansa, and I honestly was totally unaware of the history of this studio. Henric was jumping up and down with excitement. We were there for three days and it finally dawned on me how cool it was! There we could use the same machines and instruments that our heroes used. Karo: The larger stage at NCN seemed to suit you surprisingly well. Some electronic acts compensate for space by simply making every gesture bigger; with Strikkland, the additional room seemed to expose more of the interaction between you. Has playing larger stages changed the way you understand what the visual side of the band can do? Henric: We are not that used to playing larger stages. Apart from Subkultfestivalen in Sweden and WGT, most of our shows prior to NCN have been in front of a maximum of 200 to 300 people. I think there is a lot of room for visual improvement when playing the larger stages. We are just two guys and a couple of machines, so in order to put on even better shows we probably need some additional features on stage to make an impact. But we also don’t want to hide behind video walls, smoke and lasers. Guess it’s time to put on our thinking caps and find a Strikkland solution to the problem. But yeah, visuals are important to us, from album covers to how we appear on stage. Henrik: What Henric said. Karo: “Hommage” looked deliberately towards the music that made you. Looking ahead, what would be the opposite gesture? Is there something in the EBM tradition, perhaps even something you personally love, that Strikkland now need to leave behind in order to find out what the band can become next? Henrik: I can’t think of a thing in the EBM tradition that we want to leave behind. When we create new songs, all kinds of new influences colour the final result. Last time we met, the song rotated towards techno music, so who knows? I always get new ideas every time I listen to metal music. There you find my inspiration and trigger to do new stuff for Strikkland. But with that said, there will never be a guitar on stage with us. Body music forever! Henric: I don’t know, to be honest. There are most certainly no holy cows as far as Strikkland is concerned. What we would love to happen is to do even more shows in mainland Europe, and if that means we will have to tweak things one way or another, so be it. If it turns out we have to bite heads off chickens or perform in Pickelhauben in order to get booked, it might be worth a shot! I mean, a lot of people do judge books by the cover, and it would be sad to miss out because of that. We will see what happens and what we come up with. About Strikkland Strikkland are an electronic body music duo from Gothenburg, Sweden, consisting of Henric Ceder, responsible for music and programming, and Henrik Johansson, responsible for vocals and lyrics. Their first documented release, “Predatorial Right”, appeared on 27 March 2020. Their debut full-length album, “Bodypop”, followed on 2 December 2022. The ten-track record was mixed and mastered by Hans Olsson at Svenska Grammofonstudion in Gothenburg, using an analogue SSL 4000E console; Strikkland explicitly connected that production choice to their admiration for classic EBM. Their second full-length, “Hommage”, was released on 28 March 2025. The nine-track album was produced by Hans Olsson, with recording, mixing and mastering work carried out at Svenska Grammofonstudion in Gothenburg and Hansa Studios in Berlin. The band describe the album as a tribute both to the artists who inspired them and to older recording practices. They state that no AI was used in its production, relying instead primarily on classic studio equipment, hardware synthesizers and drum machines.
items._cn_summary: 瑞典哥德堡二人组Strikkland在第二张专辑《Hommage》中展现出对EBM类型的深入理解与刻意解构。专辑在制作上回归硬件设备和早期录音实践，保留硬朗的电子结构与Henrik有力的演唱方式，但通过幽默、戏谑和舞台上的夸张装扮（红色羽毛围巾、国旗等）打破EBM惯有的严肃视觉传统。两位成员明确拒绝以装扮凶悍或故作深沉来证明自身的合法性，认为对类型的真诚依附恰恰可以承载反讽与玩笑。歌词常围绕死亡、太空、幻想与荒诞展开，与现场表演的轻松态度形成持续张力。专辑不将EBM视为需要原样保存的传统遗产，而是强调传统只有在仍可被扰乱时才真正有用。这种将幽默纳入表演语言本体、以有限手段激发创造力的态度，构成专辑的核心立场。

items.body: Delerium released the single “Into The Light”, featuring Diamanda Galás, on 23 September 2026 through Metropolis Records. It is the first single from Delerium’s new album “Exaudire”, set for release on 22 January 2027. Into The Light (with Diamanda Galás) by Delerium “Into The Light” incorporates portions of “Deliver Me From Mine Enemies”, written and performed by Diamanda Galás and included on her 1986 album “The Divine Punishment”, the American avant-garde singer’s Mute Records release that opened her “Masque of the Red Death” trilogy. The Delerium track sets that material inside the group’s own production, credited to founding members Bill Leeb and Rhys Fulber. “Exaudire” follows Delerium’s 2023 album “Signs” and carries twelve tracks, continuing the group’s format of pairing largely downtempo, atmospheric songwriting with a rotating cast of guest vocalists: Higher Power (with Mimi Page) Into The Light (with Diamanda Galás) Dream Palace (with Magic Wands) Buried Light (with Mimi Page) Apocalypse (with Inna Walters) Stolen (with Phildel) Into The Unknown (with Jaël) Multiplying Zero (with Inna Walters) Chasing The Wind (with Mimi Page) Exaudire Had To Go (with Jaël) Litany (with Mimi Page) About Delerium Delerium was founded in Vancouver, Canada, in 1987 by Bill Leeb and Rhys Fulber, both already active as members of the electro-industrial group Front Line Assembly. Where Front Line Assembly carried the pair’s aggressive, rhythm-driven material, Delerium became the outlet for their dark ambient and instrumental compositions, released through Dossier and Third Mind before the project moved to Nettwerk for its commercial breakthrough. From the mid-1990s onward, starting around “Semantic Spaces” (1994), Delerium began inviting guest vocalists to front largely downtempo songs on each album, a format the group has kept since. That approach produced its best-known track, “Silence”, featuring Sarah McLachlan, which reached number three in the UK singles chart following a series of 2000 remixes and won two Juno Awards for Best Dance Recording. Delerium music has since appeared in films including “Brokedown Palace” and “Lara Croft: Tomb Raider”, and “Silence” featured more recently in the BBC drama “Industry”. With Front Line Assembly already on the Metropolis Records roster, Delerium signed to the label for the albums “Mythologie” (2016) and “Signs” (2023). “Into The Light”, featuring Diamanda Galás, is the first taste of the follow-up, “Exaudire”, due on Metropolis Records on 22 January 2027.
items._cn_summary: Delerium 即将于2027年1月通过 Metropolis Records 发行新专辑《Exaudire》，首发单曲《Into The Light》与 Diamanda Galás 合作。歌曲采样了后者1986年专辑《The Divine Punishment》中的《Deliver Me From Mine Enemies》段落，将早期美国前卫艺术声乐素材嵌入 Bill Leeb 与 Rhys Fulber 的电子制作框架中。整张专辑延续了 Delerium 一贯的慢节奏氛围化编曲路线，邀请包括 Mimi Page、Magic Wands、Phildel、Jaël 等多位客座歌手轮流主唱，形成十二首曲目。乐评以新闻稿形式发布，缺乏对音乐本身的深入评论与分析。

items.album: Rina Pavar interview: ‘Think less, be bolder’
items.excerpt: When Side-Line spoke with Rina Pavar in 2023, live performance was still something she approached from outside: the studio was familiar territory, while putting herself physically at the centre of the music remained a challenge. Three years later, watching her open Saturday at Nocturnal Culture Night on the Parkbühne, in daylight and before the festival had fully gathered momentum, the change was striking. The restraint was still there, but it no longer read as self-protection. It had become par
items.body: When Side-Line spoke with Rina Pavar in 2023, live performance was still something she approached from outside: the studio was familiar territory, while putting herself physically at the centre of the music remained a challenge. Three years later, watching her open Saturday at Nocturnal Culture Night on the Parkbühne, in daylight and before the festival had fully gathered momentum, the change was striking. The restraint was still there, but it no longer read as self-protection. It had become part of the language. That distinction matters because Pavar’s music is built around control in several senses. She writes, performs, produces and mixes her own material; her arrangements tend towards clarity rather than accumulation; and even live, the electronic architecture necessarily fixes certain parameters in advance. Yet the more interesting development is how she has begun using that control to create freedom rather than insulation. She speaks here about abandoning perfection as a useful measure, learning that a stage persona does not need to be a separate personality, and discovering that authenticity can emerge gradually rather than through some dramatic act of self-reinvention. That makes the timing of this conversation particularly interesting. Her second album, “six”, appeared in March 2025, followed later that year by “REMIXES”, which handed her tightly controlled compositions to artists including Radondo, Kay-Chi, Skelesys, New Haunts and others. In August 2026, “too much” opened another phase: more direct, more emotionally immediate and, in Pavar’s own words, less subtle. Rather than presenting this as a clean break with what came before, she seems more interested in testing how far the existing language can stretch. The final answer she gives here may be the simplest description of that process: think less, be bolder. Rina Pavar interview Karo: I saw you at NCN only a few days ago, on the Parkbühne, and I was thinking about how peculiar the setting actually was for your music: an early festival slot, daylight, people still arriving and adjusting to the day. Does a situation like that require you to construct your own atmosphere almost against the surroundings, or do you prefer not to impose a predetermined mood on a performance at all? Rina: Yes, that was really unusual. But I always take as much time as possible beforehand to rehearse and visualise the specific setting and the audience. I was familiar with NCN and the Parkbühne from a guest’s perspective, so I could easily imagine what my performance would feel and look like at that time. I think this approach allows me to adapt more flexibly to the circumstances, including in my song selection and the style of my performance. Even though, of course, the core always remains the same, the details change with every performance. Karo: When you spoke to Side-Line in 2023, performing was still relatively new territory for you and the studio was very much the place where you felt most secure. Three years later, I watched someone who seemed considerably more settled within the physical act of performing. What changed? Was it simply accumulated experience, or did you have to discover a different version of yourself onstage? Rina: I think it’s a little bit of both. So far, I still don’t approach the unknown entirely without fear or hesitation. That’s why practice and experience remain the cornerstones of my self-confidence and my progress. My stage persona has also changed over time. But through my experiences so far, I’ve realised that there’s actually no need for a “different” version of myself on stage. Rather, as my experience and self-confidence grow, more space opens up for me to enjoy the performance and let my authentic self shine through. That’s why I take the time to discover and refine myself in this environment bit by bit and at my own pace, instead of artificially building something that I’ll eventually have to shed one day because it no longer fits. Karo: “too much” arrived only a few weeks before NCN and has now been presented as the beginning of a new sequence of releases. Why was this particular song the right point of departure? What does it introduce that you felt had not already been said on six? Rina: I think it has a completely different vibe. It’s more direct, more emotional and less subtle in terms of content, without going completely over the top. At least, that’s how I feel about it. That’s why I thought it was the perfect choice for the first single. I’d actually included it in the NCN set, and the reactions were consistently positive. That confirmed my choice. Karo: six contained a great deal of looking backwards: memory, relationships, places, decisions, versions of oneself that have already existed. I wonder whether your writing is changing now from processing experience towards something more immediate. Are you becoming interested in writing from inside an experience while it is still unresolved, rather than only once you understand what it meant? Rina: For me, it always happens in a flexible and spontaneous way. When certain topics or approaches are important to me at the moment, they naturally take centre stage at that time. But things might look completely different again in the next project. Karo: Because you write, perform, produce and mix your own material, almost every important decision remains with you until the mastering stage. That gives you enormous artistic coherence, but presumably also removes the useful resistance another person can provide. How do you recognise the moment when complete creative independence stops being liberating and starts becoming a blind spot? Rina: That’s an important point. And I’ve often had to listen to all the things that can go wrong when you work on your own. That’s why I’ve found the following approach, which works for me. First, I took the pressure off myself to be perfect, and for RINA PAVAR I decided to focus on presenting what comes from me as a person, regardless of whether it’s perfect, good enough, innovative, trendy, cutting-edge or whatever. If it brings me great joy and meets my standards for growth at that moment, then that’s good enough. This creates freedom and keeps me from getting stuck in a safe, rigid framework. Furthermore, with every release, I set new but achievable goals for myself, whether musically, vocally, personally, in live performances or even just in terms of design. I sit down and teach myself something new or try to optimise processes and recognise patterns to eliminate blind spots as much as possible. Karo: There is considerable restraint in your arrangements; individual sounds are often given enough room to become structurally important rather than being surrounded by layers simply because they are available. Is reduction something you consciously work towards? In other words, do you spend as much time deciding what a song can survive without as deciding what it still needs? Rina: I think that’s one of the few things I don’t have to consciously work towards. When I’m producing a song, I actually have to force myself to add elements. I’m always surprised when someone tells me how clean or minimal the mix is. In my mind, I’ve actually “packed it full”, and I often think to myself, “Okay, there’s room for improvement here, and I should be a little bolder in approaching this aspect.” But reduction, or perhaps “clarity” is a better word, is something that runs through everything I do. For me, it’s fulfilling to break down complex situations to their essentials, to distil the core, to organise, structure or simplify things. And that happens completely automatically. Karo: REMIXES placed your songs in the hands of artists with very different instincts, which is almost the opposite of the control you normally have over your work. Was there a remix that revealed something about one of your compositions that you had not recognised yourself, perhaps because another artist emphasised a rhythm, mood or tension that you had considered secondary? Rina: I’d almost say that’s the case with all the songs. Often, my favourite elements are highlighted but placed in a completely different context or emphasised even more. I love every one of these songs and am thrilled to experience my creations in a more developed and reinterpreted form. Karo: Your collaboration with Kay-Chi on “Darkest Night” is interesting for a similar reason, because there you contributed lyrics and vocals to somebody else’s musical framework rather than building the entire environment yourself. Does writing from inside another producer’s world free you in some way, precisely because you are not responsible for every element of the finished piece? Rina: It’s definitely a challenging yet enjoyable situation. I really enjoy not having to take full responsibility for everything. At the same time, though, I often put pressure on myself to do the parts that I work on perfectly. After all, I want to do the song justice and not disappoint the artist who chose me as a collaboration partner. Even though it may seem overwhelming at first, and it’s not always easy to find my place on someone else’s song, I always look forward to projects like this. It’s fun, offers the chance to collaborate and is always a nice change of pace from working solo. Karo: You also work visually, and I am interested less in whether your visual art “matches” the music than in whether the two forms make you think differently. Music unfolds through time, while an image confronts you more or less simultaneously. Does moving between those two ways of organising an idea change the way you compose? Rina: The way I compose doesn’t change because of this. The approaches and the way ideas come to me are simply too different. But painting is my balance to music, and vice versa. For me, it’s a kind of respite from the other and therefore the break I need to develop and bring new ideas to life. Music is often stirring, full of energy and, despite studio work, takes place largely outside. Painting is absolute stillness, tranquillity, grounding and complete isolation from the outside world. Karo: Coldwave and dark electronic music have developed a very recognisable vocabulary, and recognition can become both an advantage and a trap: listeners know immediately where they are, but artists can also end up repeating gestures simply because those gestures belong to the language of the scene. Which elements of that vocabulary still feel central to Rina Pavar, and which ones have you begun questioning? Rina: If I had to name one thing that remains an important, central aspect, or an indispensable element, for me it would be the melancholy in the sound and lyrics. These are still elements of my songs because I’m still drawn to them. But to be honest, I don’t think about genre at all when I’m composing. I create songs based on the premise that “I have to like it” in order to maintain the greatest possible creative freedom. Karo: Electronic performances inevitably contain structures that cannot be altered as freely as they might be in a conventional rock band, yet the person onstage is responding to something entirely unpredictable: an audience. At NCN, how much were you actually reading the people in front of you? Can their response change the way you deliver a song even when its underlying architecture remains fixed? Rina: I can always feel the energy of the audience, and I try to respond to it as best I can. Even though the set is basically fixed, since it’s tied to a tight schedule, especially at a festival like NCN, I still always leave room within that framework to add or omit details, swap out songs, vary my vocal delivery, let loose and adjust the announcements to be longer or shorter depending on how the audience reacts. At NCN, it was great to see that everyone was fully into it even at such an early hour, and that really gave me power. Karo: Your development so far has involved becoming more confident not only as a songwriter but also as someone willing to place herself physically at the centre of the project. At this point, what would artistic growth actually mean to you? Is it greater musical complexity, greater simplicity, taking more emotional risks, collaborating more, reaching larger audiences, or something that has nothing to do with scale at all? Rina: I want to continue acquiring new technical skills and incorporating them into my compositions. When performing live, I’d like to experiment a bit more, both in terms of the performance and the look, as well as the instrumentation. It’s basically a matter of fine-tuning every aspect to bring out and strengthen the essence of RINA PAVAR even more. Karo: Finally, looking ahead: “too much” has been announced as the first of a series of new releases, so we clearly are not looking at an isolated single. Without asking you to reveal anything that should remain a surprise, what is beginning now for Rina Pavar? And when we eventually look back at this next body of work, what do you hope we will hear in it that was not there before? Rina: I do have an idea of what the “new” element will be in the upcoming releases. But since I’m always worried that listeners might not even notice it, I’d like to start by summarising it this way: Think less, be bolder. About Rina Pavar Rina Pavar is a Leipzig-based German solo project started in 2019. Her own Bandcamp describes the music as coldwave and dark electronic music, while Cold Transmission characterises the project through driving basslines, vintage synthesizers, accented vocals and lyrics concerned with consciousness and personal experience. Her debut album, “vivid night”, was released digitally on 1 November 2021, followed by the EP “things we hide” in May 2022. Pavar writes, performs, produces and mixes her own material; those credits are documented on both “vivid night” and her second album. The second album, “six”, was released through Cold Transmission on 21 March 2025. It contains nine tracks and was mastered by Frithjof Rödel at Atomino Studio, with artwork and cover by Pavar and photography by yules_pictures. On 5 December 2025, she released “REMIXES”, a ten-track collection featuring reinterpretations by Radondo, Kay-Chi, Zee Mon, Skelesys, Close Proximity, PJ, Sun’s Spectrum, New Haunts and Three Days Awake by Bent, alongside Pavar’s own club mix of “structured fall”. Pavar also contributed lyrics and vocals to Kay-Chi’s “Darkest Night”, released as part of the Night Protocol EP on 27 March 2026. Her latest single, “too much”, was released on 14 August 2026. Cold Transmission announced it as the first in a series of new releases, marking the beginning of the next phase of the project.
items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评结合采访形式，回顾了Rina Pavar从录音室创作者成长为现场表演者的历程。她包揽词曲、演奏、制作与混音，编曲追求清晰而非堆叠，电子架构为现场表演预设参数。文章聚焦于她如何将控制转化为自由而非隔离：放弃完美主义作为衡量标准，认识到舞台人格无需与本人分离，真实性可通过渐进方式浮现。2025年三月发行第二张专辑《six》，随后将作品交给Radondo、Kay-Chi、Skelesys、New Haunts等艺术家进行 remix。2026年八月发行的《too much》标志新阶段：更直接、情感更外露，她自述为'不那么微妙'。文章以NCN音乐节早期日间时段演出为切入点，探讨她在非常规表演环境下通过预演与想象构建氛围的方式。核心命题在于既有音乐语言的延展空间——'少想，更大胆'。

items.body: Like many others, my gateway into the Coltrane universe was the inevitable Blue Train , a 1997 CD reissue, with the cover altered with different tones from the original edition. I was beginning to discover jazz and, beyond the variations on the title track, it was the vertigo of “Moment’s Notice” that must have won me over at that early stage. And, of course, the free sound of the saxophone, and the fascinating process of its discourse construction in real time — fascinating for someone who, until then, knew nothing of any form of improvised music. From there, there were several landmark records, in a process that did not follow chronology: it went through the duet with Johnny Hartman, Live at Village Vanguard , the space journey of Meditations , all the way to the devotional magic of A Love Supreme , reading the booklet while following the music, and the pinnacle of Ascension . Along the way, an unavoidable landmark, Giant Steps (as with Ornette’s records, the title also announced the jazz that was coming) with its timeless title track and the melancholic sweetness of “Naima”. I was discovering the albums in no particular order, finding the records or having them find me in a random way, and then gradually organizing Coltrane’s journey in my head, as if piecing a puzzle together. In that process, my favorite album then remains my favorite to this day: My Favorite Things . Too mainstream, too easy, some might say. On ’Trane’s path, a milestone. Not yet the classic quartet, but almost there: McCoy Tyner on piano, Elvin Jones on drums, Steve Davis on bass (Jimmy Garrison would join shortly afterwards). Coltrane takes up the soprano saxophone and transforms a well-known popular melody into a piece of his own; starting from the original melody, he transforms it through a profound process of unfurling. From this point on, it would become one of his signature tunes, evolving into other, much more advanced and deconstructed versions. But this is the start. The LP setlist also has three songs that touch the soul of anyone who loves the history of jazz: one by Cole Porter, “Ev’ry Time We Say Goodbye”, and two by the Gershwins: “Summertime” and “But Not for Me”. In the context of Coltrane's quest and discography, My Favorite Things is a turning point. And, in my own listener's journey, it's music that affects me deeply. Nuno Catarino is editorial coordinator of jazz.pt since 2022. He contributes to the national newspaper Público, where he has written since 2007. He is the author, with Márcia Lessa, of the book Improvisando (2019). Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items._cn_summary: 这是一篇关于约翰·柯川百年纪念专辑《Blue Train & More》的回顾性乐评，融合了作者个人的聆听旅程。文章从《Blue Train》切入，回顾了柯川在Blue Note时期硬波普与调式爵士的根基，并延伸到《My Favorite Things》时期对流行旋律的解构与即兴重构，再到《A Love Supreme》《Ascension》等自由爵士与精神爵士的巅峰。作者详细描述了柯川在次中音与高音萨克斯上的话语建构过程，以及他与McCoy Tyner、Elvin Jones等音乐家共同塑造的经典四重奏音响。乐评文字偏重个人情感与历史回顾，对专辑本身的音乐分析较为概括，未深入探讨录音技术或新发行版本的特别之处。整体属于传统爵士范畴内的温情散文式评论。

items.body: To complement her interview in The Wire 512, Slovenian improvising pianist and bandleader Kaja Draksler creates an exclusive Wire mix Kaja Draksler studied jazz at a music-oriented high school in Ljubljana, later enrolling at the Conservatory of Amsterdam. There, her instructor, the British composer Richard Ayres, asked her the simple question,“What do you want to do?”, which set her on a path that would chafe against the jazz orthodoxy. In August Punkt.Vrt. Plastik, her long-running trio with Swedish bassist Petter Eldh and German drummer Christian Lillinger, released their fourth album, Kompress, while another of her groups, matter 100, releases its debut True Or False this October. This exclusive mix, she explains, is “more of a collage, where I mostly take excerpts from different pieces, placing them one after the other, and, at times, one of top of the other. The track selection is a mix of my own music and music I love, with a bit of a focus on piano and voices.” Tracklist Kaja Draksler “Prst, roka, laket” (excerpt) Vaqif Mustafazadə “Bizim Bakı Gecələri” (excerpt) Luciano Berio “A La Femminisca” Christian Lillinger “Poliform” (excerpt) Punkt.Vrt.Plastik “EKV” Vince Staples “Get Paid” New London Chamber Choir & James Wood “Serment” (excerpt) Georges Aperghis “Recitation 10_ left part, 1st version” Nina Simone “Who Am I” Irena Z Tomažin “Rain” (excerpt) Pauline Oliveros “Horse Sings From A Cloud” (excerpt) J Gallus “Mirabile Misterium: De Nativitate Circumcisione Et Epiphania Domini Huelgas Ensemble” matter 100 “Rushing Through The Night” (excerpt) Czajka & Puchacz “Wacky Compass” (excerpt(s)) MIA “Sunshowers” (excerpt) Cecil Taylor “Pt 4 Glossalalia” (excerpt) Craig Taborn “Glossolalia” Kaja Draksler Octet “Come See” (excerpt) Andrew Parrot “De Torrente” Judith Berkson “Castle” Ellen Arkbro “For Organ And Brass” (excerpt) matter 100 “Alternating Current” Read Peter Margasak’s full interview with Kaja Draksler in The Wire 512. items.body: Immersion What Is Lost Will Return Immersion find new shapes within familiar sounds, turning repetition into something restless What Is Lost Will Return by Immersion Given the history behind Immersion, it would be easy to hear What Is Lost Will Return as a record looking backwards. That is a useful quality for a band with Colin Newman and Malka Spigel’s respective histories: there is no shortage of past to draw upon. But What Is Lost Will Return feels pleasingly unconcerned with doing so. It occupies a strange, immediate space somewhere between song, groove and electronic abstraction, where guitars, bass, electronics and voices seem to be continually finding new combinations. ‘Nephology’ is a particularly good place to enter this world. items._cn_summary: Immersion 由 Colin Newman 与 Malka Spigel 组成，延续了 Wire 时期的后朋克血脉，但这张专辑并未陷入怀旧叙事。它将吉他、贝斯、电子与人声不断组合成新的形态，在歌曲、律动与电子抽象之间游走，开辟出一个不归属任何既定框架的中间地带。开场曲《Nephology》以沉重的贝斯脉冲作为入口，暗示整张专辑以低频驱动的节奏骨架为基础，而非旋律或人声主导。专辑的核心策略在于将熟悉的元素拆解后重新配置，让重复成为不安分的推进力，而非惰性的循环。乐器之间的对话取代了传统歌曲结构中的主从关系，电子处理模糊了原声乐器与合成音色之间的边界，整体呈现出一种冷静、克制但持续变形的声响质感。

items.body: Columbus’s Pinta, Niña and Santa María sail through “Delfín del Mundo” alongside pineapples, cockerels, chocolate, tobacco and caipirinhas, a roll call of conquest and tropical produce chanted over a psychedelic cumbia. “Delfín del Mundo” is the third and final single from Desertropical, the new EP from Dr. Rayo, due in October on Costa Rican label Lácteo Cósmico. The project belongs to Red Jesus, a Chilean-Mexican percussionist and producer who spent 2014 to 2020 on Mexico’s independent circuit. Now based in Madrid, he launched the project with a sold-out night at Moby Dick. Red Jesus made the track with Barzo, the San José-born DJ and producer who runs Lácteo Cósmico and has remixed Janelle Monáe and Erykah Badu. He came to Madrid for a short visit, and the pair recorded most of the instruments live at Dr. Rayo’s base. Barzo then built the electronic production on top of those takes. The earlier singles “Mexicali Tropical” and “Owl on Cocaine” opened big and dramatic, while “Delfín del Mundo” settles into a mid-tempo sway built on a slow-burning bassline, live percussion and a vocal delivered close to a chant. The vocal carries a message of pride in Latin American roots, and the cacao, tobacco and pineapples in the lyric were growing in the Americas long before Columbus’s ships arrived. Desertropical gets a launch party at Madrid’s Siroco at the end of September, with Spanish dates to follow in Seville, Oviedo, Gijón, Logroño and Santander. Stream “Delfín del Mundo” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Dr. Rayo x Barzo – Delfín del Mundo appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items._cn_summary: Dr. Rayo与Barzo合作的第三首单曲延续Desertropical EP的世界音乐路线。Red Jesus是一位智利-墨西哥裔打击乐手兼制作人，曾活跃于墨西哥独立音乐圈，现居马德里；Barzo则是哥斯达黎加San José出身的DJ兼厂牌主理，曾混音过Janelle Monáe与Erykah Badu的作品。制作方式上，两人先在Dr. Rayo的马德里工作室录制了大量现场乐器，再由Barzo叠加电子制作层。这首歌以哥伦布的船队与菠萝、可可、烟草等美洲原生作物并列，歌词颂唱拉丁美洲根源的自豪感。相比前两支单曲的大开大合，这首选择中速摇摆，以慢燃的低音线、现场打击乐和接近吟唱的人声构建氛围，融合迷幻cumbia与拉丁电子，呈现出殖民地历史叙事的文化反思。

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — A longtime Jazz veteran of Brasil's music scene catches the "fusion" bug, travels to the USA to collaborate with some of New York City's finest studio musicians. The album was recorded in 1970 at A&R Studios in New York City and then released by Cobblestone Records sometime later in the year.1. "Coalhada (Yogurt)" (3:00) big band jazz that happens to use electric piano. This sounds like Doc Severinson's late night band with Johnny Carson. The song's end is a fadeout during some very animated and dynamic full-band interplay. Nice full-band cohesion. (8.875/10)2. "Hermeto" (4:22) sounds like a Eumir Deodato and Burt Bacharach team rendering of "You Are the Sunshine of My Life." Hermeto's electric piano play fits so nicely over the Smooth Jazz orchestral arrangement. Nice lead flute solo from (probably) Hermeto himself. (9.125/10)3. "Guizos (Bells)" featuring Googie Coppola (6:20) gentle, atmospheric jazz stripped down to Ron Carter, Hermeto's sensual electric piano, Airto's cymbal and brush play, with Flora Purim's wordless vocalese floating within and above it--and, later, a breathy flute. The orchestra makes its presence known in bigger and bigger ways toward the end of the fourth minute, swelling just before Hermeto's sexy little keyboard dance duet with Ron. Flora and low brass return around the five minute mark, prompting the horn-led orchestra to swell again. Beautiful music (that reminds me very much of the intro "Storm at Sunup" section of Gino and Joe Vannelli's opener to their great 1974 album of the same name)! (9.12510)4. "Flor Do Amor (The Love Flower)" (5:51) opening with a beautiful small chamber arrangement of wind instruments that turns to strings for support and takeover around the 20-second mark before melding together to support a lovely lower register flute lead. The harmonic orchestral support is wonderful! Brass take over in the lead position of the "dance," giving Hermeto time to get situated at his electric piano for a turn. Then it's back to flute for the end of the fourth minute, back to keys for the fifth, dueling/dueting with flute (there are so many accomplished flute players credited in the line-up chart that it's hard for me to believe that Hermeto doesn't use one or more of them to play off of: Hubert Laws! Joe Farrell! Jerome Richardson!) (9/10)5. "Alicate (Pliers)" featuring Flora Purim (4:00) this one sounds very much like a Burt Bacharach song with the orchestra providing most of the melody leads for the first 1:45. Then an odd almost "bass" or bamboo flute enters, playing really low, really breathily. This must be Hermeto due to the Amazonian flavor/flare being presented here. Return to orchestral dominance for the rest of the third and fourth minutes (with lots of wonky, animal-sounding brass), and then fade out. (8.875/10)6. "Vel�rio (Mourning)" featuring Flora Purim (8:38) organ, bass, and low-end flute(s) and female vocalese open this one while a taped recording of tribal conversation plays beneath. The whole vibe here is one of the Amazon jungle. Even the violins that enter in the middle of the second minute and the other orchestral instruments seem to be trying to capture or emulate jungle noises. Then in the second half of the third minute Airto's lone violin-like berimbau goes completely solo, sounding like the fast-rushing of an on-coming railroad train. The fifth minute sees a return of the wooden flute (heavily reverbed), which plays solo for a complete minute before petering out and being supplanted by a faded-in piano--who continues the on-rushing train theme--until the end of the sixth minute when the orchestra's trumpet section announces itself sharply, being joined by other brass, winds, strings, and percussion instruments in a very theatric motif that begins to "fall apart" like a drunken debauch at the end of the eighth minute. The chaos is then displaced by piano, bowed bass, and tambourine playing an "old-fashioned" barroom jazz bit to the song's end. Interesting! Not my favorite but I appreciate the creativity behind the song. (17.5/20)7. "As Marianas (The Marianas)" (4:34) full orchestra playing music that sounds like the warm up music to a grand ball or art museum exhibit. This may be jazz (of the Nelson Riddle-Glen Miller kind) but it's nowhere near anything I'd apply the Jazz-Rock Fusion term to. It's also kind of lame, like a sleepy, sloppy version of "Born Free." (8.375/10)8. "Fabiula" (3:51) more "old" strings-dominated cinematic music that may be big band created (I hear the individual instruments like flutes, horns, and Spanish guitar) but it, again, fails to even come close to the musics I would term "J-R F" (or any other kind of fusion). Maybe "orchestral-bossa nova lite" would best describe this soporific fare. At least this one is far more sophisticated and melodic than the previous disaster. (8.875/10)Total time: 40:46B/four stars; Oh! how one really poor song can drag an entire album down from near-masterpiece status to good/worth your attention. Side One is definitely deserving of all your Jazz-Rock Fusion enthusiasm whereas Side Two may bore you to tears--especially if you have an aversion to languorous strings-dominated orchestral jazz and attempts to replicate the sounds of the jungle using musical instruments.

items._cn_summary: 这张1972年专辑是巴西爵士老将Hermeto Pascoal赴纽约与当地优秀录音室乐手合作的作品。整张专辑以电钢琴为核心，融入大乐队编制和管弦乐编排，带有明显的Burt Bacharach式旋律感。Airto、Flora Purim、Ron Carter等参与演奏，部分曲目呈现柔美的氛围爵士质感，搭配人声哼唱和长笛独奏。编曲层次丰富，从小型室内乐编制到完整的管弦乐铺陈均有涉及，并融入亚马逊地域色彩的低音竹笛等元素。整体制作精致，动静态段落交替有序，是一张融合巴西音乐语汇与纽约录音室爵士传统的跨界作品。

items.body: Review by alainPP — Green Carnation presents the third album in the "A Dark Poem" trilogy, nodding to the likes of Anathema and Katatonia. It delivers an oppressive, heavy, and meditative sound with dark progressive roots."Unconditional Artificial Chemistry" opens with a spacey feel, suddenly cut through by an exuberant, thick, heavy guitar; the monolithic vocals help transport the listener to another planet. The track narrates the dangers of AI, unfolding seamlessly while building an all-encompassing, progressive intensity. It shifts to include a crystalline piano in the distance, with musical grandeur that straddles the line between doom and Opeth-esque gothic metal, creating an oppressive atmosphere. There is a spellbinding melancholy'a blend of Anathema, Mogwai, Katatonia, and early King Crimson. "The Messiah Complex" features a melting guitar arpeggio, with vocals that abruptly break the ethereal, charming, and hypnotic mood. Melancholic, mysterious keyboards add a layer of solemnity that oozes progressive structure, while the dominant vocals allow the mantra-like atmosphere to spill over. The decrescendo finale is simple and effective'steady and unstoppable'serving as a musical paradigm."Broken Souls, Common Enemies" features a prominent New Wave-style synth driving the rhythm. The riff, the languid vocals, and the guitar's plaintive melody evoke emotion, discovery, and complexity in a track that is heavy without flaunting it. A shift to screamed vocals over a machine-gun riff'reminiscent of The Gathering in their early days'reasserts the track's intensity and complexity, bolstered by Wright-esque keyboards. A break featuring an ethereal flute and a melting, Western-style acoustic solo follows. Vocoded vocals amplify the majestic atmosphere, launching a stratospheric guitar solo worthy of the genre's titans'a truly stunning moment. Finally, "A Dark Poem - Orchestral Suite" begins with otherworldly vocals introducing wind instruments'including Ingrid's flute'as the orchestral arrangement takes center stage. An orchestral suite worthy of *Fantasia*'a classic pastoral anthem recounting Rimbaud's "Ophelia," performed by the Kristiansand Symphony Orchestra and its opera choir. Then comes the break: a return to archaic vocals, a primal sound reaching its zenith'is this the birth of prog? A dark, unsettling, yet colorful and pastoral atmosphere, pierced by illuminating trumpets; it is a masterpiece right up to the final note, with a soaring violin flourish creating a moment that transcends time.Green Carnation takes its final bow with this triptych finale'punchier, spellbinding, and invigorating. It is a crowning achievement, blending dystopian lyrics about our society with majestic, solemn melodies. Classy, ​​dreamlike, and immense progressive post-metal'featuring a sound that left an indelible mark on me from their very beginnings, delivering a powerful impact this September.
items._genre: experimental post-metal / progressive metal / dark metal
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是挪威乐队Green Carnation三部曲的终章，融合了Anathema式的忧郁氛围与Katatonia的沉重质感，同时借鉴了Mogwai的后摇手法与King Crimson的渐进结构。作品以反乌托邦的歌词为骨架，探讨人工智能与社会议题，在编曲上呈现极广的动态范围：从开篇的太空感失真吉他、晶体钢琴，到中段的New Wave合成器驱动、机关枪式连复段，再到管风琴般的键盘铺垫与维特风格器乐片段，层层堆叠。终曲以完整管弦乐组曲的形式收束，邀请交响乐团与歌剧院合唱团共同演绎，将兰波诗作转化为音响化的牧歌。整体兼具压迫感与冥想性，在金属的密度与古典的庄严之间寻找平衡点。

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. Various Artists - L�ve L�ve (Volume1) (Review) Pedro Lima - Maguidala (Review) Ann O'aro - Bleu (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了圣多美和普林西比两座岛屿在上世纪七十至八十年代录制的Puxa音乐。Puxa是一种融合了merengue、Kompas、Soukouss、Benga等多种节奏的复杂音乐，历史上曾因葡萄牙殖民者的禁令而被迫转入地下。这片区域是全球最小的非洲国家之一，录音资源远少于拉各斯或内罗毕等音乐重镇，因此留存下来的唱片尤为珍贵。Pedro Lima领衔的乐队展示了窒息式吉他连复段与鼓手之间的激烈交锋，Sangazuza则在贝斯与键盘退出后让鼓与吉他主导律动。多把吉他交织盘旋，主唱与和声不断呼应，使旋律框架始终饱满饱满，录音中不难还原出持续数小时的现场能量。

items.body:
A debut, digital-only EP from a Danish trio, led by one of the Nordic folk scene�s outstanding and experienced vocalists, Mia Guldhammer. Five tracks, with the musicians bringing their own perspectives to mostly traditional music. There�s a lovely ancient, creaky mood throughout.
The opener, �Svennedal,� with its rough, cantering rhythm, offers a perfect shop window for Guldhammer�s impressive, persuasive voice, while jaw harp and bagpipes bring an insistent propulsion to �Nordg�rd,� the only original here, by band member Morten Musicus.
Cimbalom adds a delicate backdrop to the traditional �Agnete Of Bjergmanden,� with Guldhammer�s soft jaw harp offering extra textures to the other instruments, as it brings a springy opening to the final cut, �Orms�,� mingling with flute and strings to create something quite thrilling and off kilter on this instrumental.
Five tracks, and an introduction to a band that already seems very mature and accomplished. A strong beginning � what will GuldGanger do with an entire album?
items.label: Go' Danish Folk Music
items._cn_summary: 这是一张来自丹麦三人组合的数字EP首作，由北欧民间音乐圈经验丰富的主唱Mia Guldhammer领衔。五首曲目大多基于传统素材进行重新演绎，呈现出一种古老而略带粗粝的氛围。开场曲以奔腾节奏展示主唱富有说服力的嗓音；唯一的原创曲目由乐队成员Morten Musicus创作，引入口簧与风笛形成强烈推进力。传统民谣在钦巴龙、口簧、长笛与弦乐的交织下获得新的层次，器乐曲在跳跃感与不安定的离调效果中收尾。作为乐队的初次亮相，五首作品已展现出超越新人水准的成熟度与完成度，为后续全长专辑留下期待空间。整体定位介于传统北欧民谣与世界音乐之间，在传统框架内注入了跨界编排的巧思。

items._cn_summary: 本文是Dusted杂志对近期几张专辑的简短评论合集。James Brandon Lewis的《Red Lily – Calling Antonín》以德沃夏克为灵感，在室内乐质地与自由爵士之间游走，次中音萨克斯与小号、鼓、贝斯、大提琴、中提琴形成多元编制对话。The Yummy Fur的新作《Everybody Talks About the Weather》也有涉及，但原文截断，信息有限。整体而言，这是汇总性的资讯转载而非深度乐评，所提及的Lewis专辑在学院派爵士与前卫即兴的交汇点上有一定探索价值，但文章本身未能展开更多音乐分析。

The show, which was Mills play all-vinyl, formed part of his tour around the world in support of the 30th anniversary reissue of his classic Live At The Liquid Room, Tokyo mix compilation last year. The set was recorded in Spatial Audio using 14 microphones that Apple Music set up around Knockdown Center. It's been split into two parts, with the first part available for streaming now alongside a Ken Ishii mix... items._cn_summary: 底特律老牌Techno制作人Jeff Mills通过Apple Music发布了一组纽约Knockdown Center的现场录音，时长分为两部分。这是他去年纪念《Live At The Liquid Room, Tokyo》合辑发行30周年的全球巡演一站，整场演出采用全黑胶播放方式完成。录音使用14支话筒进行空间音频采集，试图在数字平台上重现俱乐部声场环境。内容侧重于录音技术与发行渠道的新闻性描述，对实际音乐风格、曲目编排及声音特征的评论较少。作为纯粹的俱乐部Techno现场，与用户偏好的实验/前卫/即兴/暗潮等方向存在一定距离，但作为电子音乐范畴内的现场记录仍有一定参考价值。

Spanning six tracks, hotel room has its roots in a residency by the two artists at the 2023 Kraków edition of Unsound. The two artists met for the residency and exchanged ideas that birthed the record, which takes in three long-form pieces and three shorter cuts. From there, they worked in isolation with the drafts they had made, before rousay handled the final mixdown of the material for the album. Speaking about the lengths of the tracks that they made, Basta said: "It wasn’t something we specifically planned. It just unfolded that way." The duo will present... The post claire rousay and Martyna Basta Combine on New Album for Unsound, ‘hotel room’ appeared first on The Quietus.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Claire Rousay与Martyna Basta的合作成果，源自2023年克拉科夫Unsound音乐节的驻留项目。两位艺术家在驻留期间交换想法，随后各自独立发展素材，最终由Rousay负责混音完成。专辑包含六首作品，其中三首为长篇幅，另三首为较短曲目，长度差异并非刻意设计，而是自然形成的结果。整张专辑基于两位艺术家各自独立工作的模式构建，反映了当代实验音乐中常见的远程协作与素材交换的创作流程。作为Unsound厂牌旗下的发行作品，它延续了该厂牌关注前沿实验音乐的定位。
